docs.title: Programming in R
docs.text: Welcome to programming in R, introduction course!

docs.title: What is R?
docs.text: R is a powerful programming language and software environment specifically designed for statistical computing and graphics. Originally developed in the early 1990s by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman at the University of Auckland, New Zealand, R was created as an open-source implementation of the S programming language developed at Bell Labs.

docs.title: A Brief History of R
docs.text:
The story of R begins with the S language, which was developed by John Chambers and colleagues at Bell Laboratories starting in 1976. S was revolutionary for its time, providing statisticians with a flexible environment for data analysis and visualisation.

In 1991, Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman began developing R as a free alternative to S. They named it "R" partly as a play on their first names and partly as a tribute to the S language. The first official version of R was released in 1995, and by 1997, R became a GNU project with a core development team known as the "R Core Team."

Today, R is maintained by the R Foundation for Statistical Computing and has grown into one of the most widely used programming languages in data science, with over 18,000 packages available on CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network).

docs.title: Why R is Essential for Modern Biology
1. Built for Statistics and Data Analysis
docs.text: Biology has become increasingly data-driven, with genomics, ecology, and experimental biology generating massive datasets. R was designed from the ground up for statistical analysis, making it the perfect tool for biological research.

docs.title: 2. Specialized Biological Packages
docs.text:
The R ecosystem includes thousands of packages specifically designed for biological applications:

  • Phylogenetics: Tools for evolutionary analysis (ape, phytools, geiger)
  • Ecology: Packages for community ecology, species distribution modeling, and biodiversity analysis
  • Genomics: Advanced tools for sequence analysis, gene expression, and population genetics

docs.title: 3. Publication-Quality Graphics
docs.text: R excels at creating publication-ready visualisations. From simple scatter plots to complex heatmaps and phylogenetic trees, R's graphics capabilities (especially with ggplot2) are unmatched in the scientific community.

docs.title: 4. Reproducible Research
docs.text: R integrates seamlessly with tools like R Markdown and Quarto, allowing scientists to create reproducible research documents that combine code, results, and narrative text. This is crucial for scientific transparency and collaboration.

docs.title: 5. Open Source and Free
docs.text: Unlike expensive statistical software packages, R is completely free and open source. This makes it accessible to researchers worldwide, regardless of institutional budgets.

docs.title: 6. Active Community
docs.text: The R community is particularly strong in academia and biological sciences. This means extensive documentation, tutorials, and support specifically relevant to biological applications.

docs.title: What You'll Learn in This Course
docs.text:
Throughout this course, you'll develop practical R skills that directly apply to biological research:

  • Basic programming concepts in R
  • Data import, cleaning, and manipulation
  • Working with biological datasets
  • Data visualisation and graphical communication
  • Statistical analysis and hypothesis testing
  • Creating reproducible analyses

Whether you're analysing gene expression data, conducting ecological surveys, or running behavioural experiments, the skills you learn here will be invaluable throughout your scientific career.

docs.title: Good coding practice
docs.text:
Keep your code clean and tidy by making use of comments and white space and respecting the style guide. Comments start with the character # (R simply does not interpret anything written between a comment sign and the end of the line. They allow you to annotate your code, i.e. to write helpful notes in between all the raw program code. Notice also that white space such as empty lines, spaces and indentations (obtained by pressing the Tab key) are invisible to R. Making good use of white space helps keep your code readable, and so does using clear and descriptive variable names.

The following two examples make this point clear. Both programs do exactly the same thing, but one will make sense one year from now, and the other will not!

docs.title: Example 1
docs.text:
boooom <-0.01
blah2          =0.005
    blah3<- 0.0036
bigblah                           = boooom+ blah2        + blah3
tadayeahmanfunky<-100*exp(bigblah*10)
tadayeahmanfunky

docs.title: Example 2
docs.text:
#--------------------------------
# Program:     population_size.R
# Author:      Bob Verity
# Date:        2021-10-01
# Purpose:
# Works out the size of a population under a simple model of exponential growth.
# The growth rate is assumed to be equal to the sum of the nutrient content (% sugars),
# the temperature (centigrade above 20), and the humidity (%).
# Other parameters include the starting population size (number of individuals)
# and the time allowed to grow (hours).
#--------------------------------

# Define input parameters
nutrients     <- 0.01
temperature   <- 0.005
humidity      <- 0.0036
starting_size <- 100
grow_time     <- 10

# Calculate total growth rate
growth_rate <- nutrients + temperature + humidity

# Calculate population size at the end of the time period
end_size <- starting_size * exp(growth_rate * grow_time)

# Return end population size in the console
end_size
#--------------------------------

docs.title: Practical 3 - Functions, Flow Control, and Defensive Programming
Introduction
docs.text:
In Practicals 1 and 2, you learned how to manipulate atomic vectors and composite data structures (matrices, lists, and data frames) using vectorized expressions. In this practical, we shift from executing one-off interactive commands to constructing modular, reusable computational software.

In modern ecological research and environmental data science, scripts must be transparent, testable, and robust against unexpected inputs. You will learn to:

  1. Encapsulate scientific logic into custom functions with formal arguments, sensible defaults, and controlled return values.
  2. Implement defensive programming by validating input types, checking bounds, and halting execution with informative error messages (stop()).
  3. Control execution flow using scalar conditional branching (if / else if / else).
  4. Automate repetitive computations using pre-allocated loops (for / while), including iteration skips (next) and early loop termination (break).
  5. Translate multi-step ecological problem descriptions into modular pipelines of functions.

We will focus on deterministic algorithms—stochastic simulations and pseudo-random numbers will be introduced in Practical 4.

docs.title: The Anatomy of an R Function
docs.text:
A function is an encapsulated, named block of code that accepts inputs (arguments), executes a set of instructions, and returns an output object.

Functions provide three decisive advantages in scientific programming:

  • Elimination of Duplication: You write and debug a mathematical calculation once, rather than copying and pasting lines across your script.
  • Isolation (Scope): Variables created inside a function exist only during its execution. They do not overwrite variables in your global workspace.
  • Testability: You can systematically test a function against edge cases and boundary conditions to ensure its computational correctness.

docs.title: Basic Syntax and Return Values
docs.text:
Functions are created using the function keyword and assigned to a variable name using <-:

# Define a function to calculate acoustic sound velocity in seawater (Mackenzie, 1981):
calc_sound_speed <- function(temp_c, salinity_psu, depth_m) {
  speed <- 1448.96 + 4.591 * temp_c - 0.05304 * (temp_c^2) + 
           1.340 * (salinity_psu - 35.0) + 0.0163 * depth_m
  return(speed)
}

To execute (call) the function, pass the arguments by position or by name:

# By position:
calc_sound_speed(12.5, 34.2, 250.0)

# By name (preferred for clarity and order independence):
calc_sound_speed(depth_m = 250.0, temp_c = 12.5, salinity_psu = 34.2)

Rules of Return:

  1. In R, return(value) explicitly terminates the function and passes value back to the caller.
  2. If return() is omitted, R automatically returns the last evaluated expression in the function body. However, in scientific programming, writing explicit return() statements makes your exit points unambiguous.
  3. A function can return only one single object. If you need to return multiple pieces of information (e.g., a numeric summary, a filtered data frame, and a status flag), package them into a named list.

docs.title: Default Arguments
docs.text:
You can provide fallback default values for arguments in the function header:

calc_hydrostatic_pressure <- function(depth_m, gravity = 9.80665, water_density = 1025.0) {
  # pressure in kiloPascals (kPa)
  pressure_kpa <- (water_density * gravity * depth_m) / 1000.0
  return(pressure_kpa)
}

# Uses defaults for gravity and water density:
calc_hydrostatic_pressure(depth_m = 100.0)

# Overrides water density for a freshwater lake:
calc_hydrostatic_pressure(depth_m = 100.0, water_density = 1000.0)

docs.title: Variable Scoping: Local vs Global
docs.text:
Consider this scenario:

calibration_offset <- 1.5

adjust_reading <- function(reading) {
  adjusted <- reading + calibration_offset
  return(adjusted)
}

adjust_reading(10.0)  # Returns 11.5

The function was able to find calibration_offset in the global environment even though it was not passed as an argument. This is dangerous practice. If calibration_offset is renamed, modified, or cleared from memory later in your session, your function will break or return incorrect numbers without warning.

Golden Rule of Modularity: A function should be a self-contained "black box". It should rely only on arguments explicitly passed into it and variables defined locally within its body.

docs.title: Q1. Consider the function:
docs.text:
estimate_heat_content <- function(temp_c, water_mass_kg, specific_heat = 4184) {
  joules <- water_mass_kg * specific_heat * temp_c
  return(joules)
}
  1. What value is returned by estimate_heat_content(20.0, 50.0)?
  2. If you evaluate joules in your console after running this function, what happens? Why?

docs.title: Defensive Programming and Input Validation
docs.text:
When writing scripts for your own use, you might know what inputs are expected. However, in larger models, shared repositories, and automated pipelines, functions frequently receive incorrect, incomplete, or corrupted inputs.

Defensive programming means designing your function to inspect its arguments before performing calculations, verifying that all preconditions hold, and immediately halting with an informative error if an inconsistency is detected.

docs.title: Halting Execution with stop()
docs.text:
The stop() function interrupts execution immediately, aborts any ongoing calculations, and prints an error message to the console:

validate_temperature <- function(temp_c) {
  if (temp_c < -273.15) {
    stop("Input temperature cannot be below absolute zero (-273.15 C).")
  }
  return(temp_c + 273.15)
}

validate_temperature(-300.0)
# Error in validate_temperature(-300): Input temperature cannot be below absolute zero (-273.15 C).

docs.title: Essential Validation Checks
docs.text:
Every robust scientific function should validate its inputs against four structural criteria:

  1. Dimensionality / Length: Is the input a single scalar, or a vector of expected length? 
    if (length(x) != 1) {
  stop("Argument 'x' must be a scalar (vector of length 1).")
}
  2. Data Type / Class: Does the input conform to the required atomic class? 
    if (!is.numeric(x)) {
  stop("Argument 'x' must be numeric.")
}
  3. Missingness: Does the input contain forbidden NA or NaN values? 
    if (is.na(x)) {
  stop("Argument 'x' cannot be NA.")
}
  4. Physical / Logical Bounds: Do the values fall within valid operational limits? 
    if (x <= 0) {
  stop("Argument 'x' must be strictly positive.")
}

docs.title: Combining Validation Checks
docs.text:
Let us build a validated function that computes dissolved oxygen saturation concentration:

calc_do_saturation <- function(temp_c, salinity_psu = 35.0) {
  # 1. Check types
  if (!is.numeric(temp_c) || !is.numeric(salinity_psu)) {
    stop("All arguments must be numeric.")
  }

  # 2. Check scalar lengths
  if (length(temp_c) != 1 || length(salinity_psu) != 1) {
    stop("Inputs must be single scalar values.")
  }

  # 3. Check for NA
  if (is.na(temp_c) || is.na(salinity_psu)) {
    stop("Inputs cannot be NA.")
  }

  # 4. Check domain bounds
  if (temp_c < -2.0 || temp_c > 45.0) {
    stop("Temperature out of realistic environmental range (-2.0 C to 45.0 C).")
  }
  if (salinity_psu < 0.0 || salinity_psu > 50.0) {
    stop("Salinity must be between 0.0 and 50.0 PSU.")
  }

  # Calculation proceeds safely:
  sat_conc <- 14.6 - 0.4 * temp_c + 0.008 * (temp_c^2) - 0.05 * salinity_psu
  return(sat_conc)
}

Note on || vs | in Conditions: When testing conditions inside a scalar if statement, R provides the double operators && (short-circuit AND) and || (short-circuit OR). Unlike & and | (which evaluate element-by-element across vectors), && and || evaluate only single logical expressions from left to right and halt evaluation as soon as the truth value is determined. Always use && and || inside if statements.

docs.title: Q2. Inspect the following function:
docs.text:
calc_dilution_factor <- function(stock_conc, target_conc) {
  if (target_conc >= stock_conc) {
    stop("Target concentration must be strictly less than stock concentration.")
  }
  return(stock_conc / target_conc)
}

What happens if someone evaluates calc_dilution_factor(stock_conc = "100", target_conc = 10)? What additional defensive check is required to prevent an unexpected failure?

docs.title: Flow Control: Conditional Branching
docs.text: Conditional branching allows your code to make decisions, executing different blocks of instructions depending on whether a given condition evaluates to TRUE or FALSE.

docs.title: Syntax of if, else if, and else
docs.text:
classify_water_layer <- function(depth_m) {
  if (depth_m < 0) {
    stop("Depth cannot be negative.")
  }

  if (depth_m <= 200.0) {
    zone <- "Epipelagic"
  } else if (depth_m <= 1000.0) {
    zone <- "Mesopelagic"
  } else if (depth_m <= 4000.0) {
    zone <- "Bathypelagic"
  } else {
    zone <- "Abyssopelagic"
  }

  return(zone)
}

Execution runs sequentially:

  1. R evaluates the condition in the initial if. If TRUE, it executes that code block and skips the rest of the chain.
  2. If FALSE, it moves to the first else if. It tests each subsequent condition until one evaluates to TRUE.
  3. If none of the conditions evaluate to TRUE, the fallback else block executes.

docs.title: Resolving Missing States in Comparisons
docs.text:
Because comparing an unknown value to a number yields NA (for instance, NA > 5 evaluates to NA), passing NA into a standard if statement will trigger an error: Error in if (x > 5) : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed.

You must explicitly test for missingness using is.na() before performing numeric comparisons:

# Model the establishment of a colonising species arriving at a survey site:
resolve_site_occupancy <- function(colonist_density, resident_density) {
  # Scenario A: The habitat patch is completely unoccupied
  if (is.na(resident_density)) {
    final_density <- colonist_density
  # Scenario B: The habitat patch is already occupied
  } else if (colonist_density > resident_density) {
    final_density <- colonist_density  # Colonist outcompetes resident
  } else {
    final_density <- resident_density  # Resident resists invasion
  }

  return(final_density)
}

resolve_site_occupancy(colonist_density = 15.2, resident_density = NA)    # 15.2
resolve_site_occupancy(colonist_density = 12.0, resident_density = 18.5) # 18.5
resolve_site_occupancy(colonist_density = 22.4, resident_density = 18.5) # 22.4

docs.title: Q3. Write a function named clamp_reading that takes three arguments: val, lower, and upper.
docs.text:
1. The function should verify that lower < upper. If not, halt with stop().
  2. If val is strictly below lower, return lower.
  3. If val is strictly above upper, return upper.
  4. Otherwise, return val.

docs.title: Flow Control: Iteration with Loops
docs.text: While R favors vectorized operations for simple array transformations, iterative algorithms, step-by-step dynamical models, and multi-stage simulations require explicit control loops.

docs.title: The for Loop
docs.text:
A for loop executes a block of code once for each element in an index sequence:

station_depths <- c(15.0, 45.0, 120.0, 310.0)

for (d in station_depths) {
  cat("Processing station at depth:", d, "meters\n")
}

docs.title: Index-Based Loops and Vector Pre-Allocation
docs.text: In scientific programming, you routinely use loops to populate a vector or table with calculated outputs.

docs.title: The Anti-Pattern: Dynamic Growth (Avoid)
docs.text:
# INEFFICIENT:
results <- c()  # Empty vector
for (i in 1:1000) {
  results <- c(results, i * 2)  # Re-allocates memory on every iteration!
}

Every time you call c(results, ...), R has to allocate a completely new chunk of memory in RAM, copy the entire existing vector into it, append the new value, and delete the old chunk. For large loops, this causes severe slowdowns.

docs.title: The Correct Pattern: Vector Pre-Allocation
docs.text:
Always allocate the destination vector with its known final length before entering the loop, and populate values directly by index:

n_steps <- 5
# Pre-allocate numeric vector of length 5 filled with NA:
simulated_profile <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = n_steps)
# Alternatively: rep(NA_real_, n_steps)

for (i in seq_len(n_steps)) {
  simulated_profile[i] <- 10.0 + 2.5 * (i^1.5)
}

simulated_profile

Safe Indexing with seq_len() and seq_along(): Avoid writing for (i in 1:length(vec)). If vec happens to be empty (length 0), R evaluates 1:0, creating a sequence c(1, 0) that runs two buggy iterations. Instead, use:

  • seq_len(n): Generates 1:n, or an empty sequence if n == 0.
  • seq_along(vec): Generates indices matching the exact elements of vec, handling empty vectors safely.

docs.title: The while Loop
docs.text:
A while loop continues executing as long as its condition evaluates to TRUE. It is ideal when you do not know in advance how many iterations are required—such as iterating until a population converges to equilibrium or a numerical tolerance is satisfied:

current_val <- 100.0
decay_rate  <- 0.85
step_count  <- 0

# Iterate until the substance decays below 10.0:
while (current_val >= 10.0) {
  current_val <- current_val * decay_rate
  step_count  <- step_count + 1
}

cat("Decayed below threshold in", step_count, "steps. Final value:", current_val, "\n")

Guard Against Infinite Loops: If the condition of a while loop never becomes FALSE, your script will hang indefinitely. Always ensure the loop variable is modified inside the body, or include a maximum iteration counter with a break statement.

docs.title: Controlling Loop Execution: next and break
docs.text:
• next: Immediately skips the remainder of the current loop iteration and advances to the next step.
  • break: Immediately terminates the loop, jumping out to the code following the loop block.
measured_temperatures <- c(14.2, -999.0, 16.8, 15.5, -999.0, 18.2)
calibrated_temps <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(measured_temperatures))

for (i in seq_along(measured_temperatures)) {
  current_reading <- measured_temperatures[i]

  # Skip corrupted sensor codes (-999.0):
  if (current_reading == -999.0) {
    calibrated_temps[i] <- NA
    next
  }

  # Process valid readings:
  calibrated_temps[i] <- current_reading * 1.02 + 0.1
}

calibrated_temps
# 14.584     NA 17.236 15.910     NA 18.664
