docs.title: Practical Review Exercises
docs.text: Work through these multi-step exercises in your R script. Focus on translating ecological descriptions into clear, defensive functions and structured iterative code.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Dynamic Harvest Quotas and Fisheries Escapement
docs.text:
In fisheries conservation, sustainable yield policies often employ biological escapement thresholds. Instead of allowing a fixed annual catch, fisheries managers adjust the permitted quota based on the estimated adult biomass at the start of the season.

Consider a coastal cod stock managed under a three-tier harvest control rule:

  1. Moratorium Tier: If adult biomass $B$ is below the critical threshold $B_{crit} = 1500\text{ tonnes}$, no fishing is permitted (harvest $H = 0$).
  2. Proportional Tier: If biomass is between $B_{crit}$ and the target threshold $B_{targ} = 5000\text{ tonnes}$, harvest is set to: $$H = 0.20 \times (B - B_{crit})$$
  3. Maximum Sustainable Tier: If biomass is at or above $B_{targ}$, the harvest rate is capped at: $$H = 0.20 \times (B_{targ} - B_{crit}) + 0.35 \times (B - B_{targ})$$

Furthermore, under adverse environmental conditions (e.g., poor marine heatwave years), harvest rates must be reduced by an additional conservation buffer.

docs.title: Part A: Single-Season Harvest Decision Function
docs.text:
Write a function named calc_harvest_quota that accepts the following arguments:

  • biomass: Estimated adult biomass in tonnes.
  • marine_heatwave: Logical scalar indicating whether a severe heatwave occurred during the spawning season (defaults to FALSE).
  • b_crit: Critical threshold (defaults to 1500.0).
  • b_targ: Target threshold (defaults to 5000.0).

The function must execute these steps:

  1. Defensive Validation:
    • Verify that biomass is a single numeric scalar and is strictly non-negative ($\ge 0$). If violated, halt execution with stop().
    • Verify that marine_heatwave is a single logical scalar (TRUE or FALSE).
    • Verify that b_crit < b_targ.
  2. Harvest Determination:
    • Calculate the base harvest $H$ using the three-tier rule above.
    • If marine_heatwave == TRUE and $H > 0$, apply a $25\%$ reduction to the calculated harvest ($H_{adj} = 0.75 \times H$).
    • Ensure the final harvest never exceeds the available biomass ($H \le B$).
  3. Return Value:
    • Return the final permitted catch as a single numeric scalar.

Test your function with the following calls and check the outputs:

calc_harvest_quota(biomass = 1200)                         # Should return 0
calc_harvest_quota(biomass = 3500)                         # 0.20 * (3500 - 1500) = 400
calc_harvest_quota(biomass = 3500, marine_heatwave = TRUE) # 400 * 0.75 = 300
calc_harvest_quota(biomass = 6000)                         # 0.20 * 3500 + 0.35 * 1000 = 1050

docs.title: Part B: Multi-Year Stock Trajectory Simulation
docs.text:
Write a second function named simulate_fishery_trajectory with the signature:

simulate_fishery_trajectory <- function(b_start, years, intrinsic_growth = 0.35, carrying_capacity = 8000)

The function simulates population changes from year $t$ to year $t+1$ using a logistic growth model with harvest: $$B_{t+1} = B_t + r B_t \left(1 - \frac{B_t}{K}\right) - H_t$$ where $r = \text{intrinsic_growth}$, $K = \text{carrying_capacity}$, and $H_t$ is determined by calling calc_harvest_quota(biomass = B_t).

Requirements:

  1. Validate that years is a single integer-like numeric value $\ge 1$.
  2. Pre-allocate a numeric vector named biomass_history of length years + 1. Set biomass_history[1] <- b_start.
  3. Pre-allocate a numeric vector named harvest_history of length years.
  4. Using a for loop over years $1, \dots, \text{years}$:
    • Determine $H_t$ from the current stock level using calc_harvest_quota(). Store it in harvest_history[t].
    • Compute the post-harvest biomass at year $t+1$.
    • Extinction check: If calculated biomass falls below $1.0\text{ tonne}$, set the biomass to $0.0$, record the remaining years as $0.0$, and terminate the loop immediately using break.
  5. Package the results into a named list containing:
    • biomass: The full trajectory vector.
    • harvest: The vector of catches.
    • collapsed: A logical flag indicating whether the stock collapsed to zero.
  6. Return the list.

Verify your function by running a 20-year simulation starting at $B_0 = 2000$:

sim_run <- simulate_fishery_trajectory(b_start = 2000, years = 20)
sim_run$collapsed
head(sim_run$biomass)

docs.title: Exercise 2: The Discrete-Time Logistic Map & Non-Linear Population Regimes
docs.text:
A classic foundation of theoretical population biology is Robert May's (1976) analysis of the discrete-time logistic difference equation:

$$x_{t+1} = r \, x_t \, (1 - x_t)$$

Here, $x_t$ represents the population density scaled between $0.0$ and $1.0$ (as a fraction of carrying capacity), and $r$ is the intrinsic reproductive rate ($0 < r \le 4.0$). Despite its mathematical simplicity, this equation exhibits diverse dynamical regimes—from stable equilibrium, to periodic cycle doubling, to deterministic chaos.

docs.title: Part A: The Logistic Step Function
docs.text:
Write a function named logistic_step that computes a single step:

logistic_step <- function(x, r)
  1. Validation:
    • Verify that both x and r are single numeric scalars.
    • Verify that $0.0 \le x \le 1.0$. If violated, halt with stop("x must be in [0, 1].").
    • Verify that $r > 0.0$ and $r \le 4.0$. If violated, halt with stop("r must be in (0, 4].").
  2. Compute and return the value of $x_{t+1} = r x (1 - x)$.

docs.title: Part B: Time-Series Generator
docs.text:
Write a function named iterate_logistic_map with the signature:

iterate_logistic_map <- function(x0, r, n_steps)
  1. Validate that n_steps is a single positive integer $\ge 1$.
  2. Pre-allocate a numeric vector trajectory of length n_steps + 1.
  3. Set trajectory[1] <- x0.
  4. Using a for loop, iteratively call logistic_step() to generate values for $t = 1, \dots, n_steps$.
  5. Return the full trajectory vector.

Test your function: 

traj <- iterate_logistic_map(x0 = 0.2, r = 2.8, n_steps = 50)
length(traj)    # Should be 51
tail(traj, 5)   # Should settle around ~0.6428

docs.title: Part C: Testing for Asymptotic Convergence to a Fixed Point
docs.text:
When $r \le 3.0$, the logistic map converges to a single stable fixed point. Above $r \approx 3.0$, the dynamics bifurcate into oscillations.

Write a function named check_fixed_point_convergence that tests whether a trajectory has converged:

check_fixed_point_convergence <- function(x0, r, burn_in = 200, eval_window = 20, tolerance = 1e-4)
  1. Run the map for total_steps = burn_in + eval_window steps using iterate_logistic_map().
  2. Extract the tail of the simulation corresponding to the evaluation window (the last eval_window elements).
  3. Compute the absolute differences between consecutive values in this window: $$\Delta_t = |x_t - x_{t-1}|$$
  4. Check if the maximum absolute difference across the window is strictly less than tolerance:
    • If $\max(\Delta) < \text{tolerance}$, the system has converged to a single fixed point. Return TRUE.
    • Otherwise, the system is oscillating or chaotic. Return FALSE.

Test your convergence checker: 

check_fixed_point_convergence(x0 = 0.3, r = 2.6)  # Should return TRUE (stable point)
check_fixed_point_convergence(x0 = 0.3, r = 3.2)  # Should return FALSE (2-point cycle)
check_fixed_point_convergence(x0 = 0.3, r = 3.8)  # Should return FALSE (chaos)

docs.title: Part D: Parameter Scan Across Reproductive Rates
docs.text:
Now, write a script to evaluate how the long-term dynamical regime shifts across reproductive rates:

  1. Create a sequence of 60 evenly spaced $r$ values between $2.5$ and $3.7$: 
    r_values <- seq(from = 2.5, to = 3.7, length.out = 60)
  2. Pre-allocate a logical vector is_stable of length 60, filled with NA.
  3. Pre-allocate a numeric vector asymptotic_mean of length 60, filled with NA.
  4. Using a for loop over seq_along(r_values):
    • Evaluate check_fixed_point_convergence(x0 = 0.2, r = r_values[i]) and store the result in is_stable[i].
    • Generate a 300-step trajectory with that $r$. Compute the arithmetic mean of the last 30 steps and store it in asymptotic_mean[i].
  5. Display the proportion of scanned $r$ values that yield stable fixed-point dynamics using mean(is_stable).
  6. Identify the largest value of $r$ in your sequence for which the system remained stable: 
    max(r_values[is_stable])

docs.title: Exercise 3: Wetland Microclimate & Thermal Buffering Model
docs.text: Wetland vegetation canopies buffer local microclimates against extreme atmospheric heat. An ecological biophysics model predicts water temperature in shaded reed beds based on ambient air temperature and water flow velocity.

docs.title: Problem Formulation
docs.text:
At hourly time steps, the change in wetland water temperature ($T_{w}$) depends on thermal transfer from air ($T_a$) and convective cooling from inflow velocity ($v$, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$):

$$\Delta T_w = k_{air} \times (T_a - T_w) - k_{flow} \times v \times (T_w - T_{inflow})$$

where: * $k_{air} = 0.12$ (air-water heat transfer coefficient) * $k_{flow} = 0.25$ (flow convective coefficient) * $T_{inflow} = 12.0\,^\circ\text{C}$ (temperature of upstream groundwater spring)

If the calculated water temperature exceeds a critical ecological threshold ($T_{crit} = 22.0\,^\circ\text{C}$), dissolved oxygen stress occurs.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Write a function named update_wetland_temp: 

    update_wetland_temp <- function(current_tw, air_temp, flow_velocity, k_air = 0.12, k_flow = 0.25, inflow_temp = 12.0)

    • Validate that all inputs are single numeric scalars.
    • If flow_velocity < 0, halt execution with stop("Flow velocity cannot be negative.").
    • Calculate $\Delta T_w$ and return the updated temperature $T_{w} + \Delta T_w$.

  2. Write an iterative simulation function named simulate_heatwave_impact: 

    simulate_heatwave_impact <- function(initial_tw, air_temp_profile, flow_velocity)

  3. air_temp_profile: A numeric vector representing hourly air temperatures over a heatwave event.
  4. initial_tw: Water temperature at hour 0.
  5. flow_velocity: Inflow velocity throughout the event.

The function must: * Validate that air_temp_profile has length at least 1 and contains no NA values. * Pre-allocate a numeric vector water_temps to store temperatures at each hour. * Iterate through the hours using a for loop, updating the water temperature sequentially using update_wetland_temp(). * Count the total number of hours where the water temperature was strictly above $22.0\,^\circ\text{C}$. * Package and return a named list containing: * hourly_temps: The full vector of simulated water temperatures. * max_water_temp: The maximum temperature reached. * stress_hours: Total hours exceeding $22.0\,^\circ\text{C}$. * buffered: A logical scalar that is TRUE if max_water_temp remained below the maximum air temperature observed in air_temp_profile.

  1. Test your simulation using a 24-hour sinusoidal heatwave profile: 
    hours <- 1:24
heatwave_air <- 20.0 + 8.0 * sin((hours - 8) * pi / 12)

# Run simulation under stagnant flow (v = 0.02 m/s):
low_flow_run <- simulate_heatwave_impact(initial_tw = 14.0, air_temp_profile = heatwave_air, flow_velocity = 0.02)

# Run simulation under active flushing flow (v = 0.15 m/s):
high_flow_run <- simulate_heatwave_impact(initial_tw = 14.0, air_temp_profile = heatwave_air, flow_velocity = 0.15)

cat("Low flow stress hours:", low_flow_run$stress_hours, "\n")
cat("High flow stress hours:", high_flow_run$stress_hours, "\n")

docs.title: Exercise 4: Multi-Site Invasiveness & Reserve Threat Scoring Pipeline
docs.text:
Conservation managers evaluate habitat patches for invasive weed colonization risk. The vulnerability of a patch depends on canopy openness, visitor footfall, and distance to the nearest road corridor.

You are provided with records from 6 protected nature reserves:

reserve_names   <- c("Glen_Caladh", "Coed_Cariad", "Cairn_Moss", "Firth_Fen", "Dune_Reach", "Alder_Meadow")
canopy_cover    <- c(0.85, 0.40, 0.15, 0.90, 0.25, 0.60)     # Fractional canopy cover (0 to 1)
visitor_density <- c(12.5, 45.0, 8.0, 3.5, 62.0, 28.0)       # Visitors per hectare per day
road_dist_km    <- c(4.2, 0.8, 12.0, 6.5, 0.3, 1.9)          # Distance to nearest road
is_peatland     <- c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)  # Peat soils have unique acidity

docs.title: Part A: Patch Vulnerability Index Function
docs.text:
Write a function named calculate_patch_vulnerability that calculates a threat index ($V$) for a single site:

calculate_patch_vulnerability <- function(canopy, visitors, road_dist, peatland)

The ecological scoring rules are:

  1. Precondition Checks:
    • Verify all inputs are single values of the correct class (numeric for the first three, logical for peatland).
    • Verify that $0 \le \text{canopy} \le 1$.
    • Verify that visitors >= 0 and road_dist >= 0.
  2. Base Risk Calculation:
    • Open canopies receive more light, accelerating invasive plant germination: $$\text{light_score} = 1.0 - \text{canopy}$$
    • Roads act as seed dispersal corridors; closer roads increase vulnerability: $$\text{corridor_risk} = \frac{1.0}{1.0 + \text{road_dist}}$$
    • Base vulnerability combines light and road proximity weighted by human traffic: $$V = (0.6 \times \text{light_score} + 0.4 \times \text{corridor_risk}) \times (1.0 + 0.05 \times \text{visitors})$$
  3. Soil Modifier:
    • If peatland == TRUE, the acidic soil suppresses most generalist plant invaders. Apply a $40\%$ reduction ($V_{final} = 0.60 \times V$).
    • Otherwise, $V_{final} = V$.
  4. Return $V_{final}$ rounded to 3 decimal places.

docs.title: Part B: Reserve Registry and Batch Threat Evaluation
docs.text:
Write a function named audit_reserve_network that processes all candidate reserves:

audit_reserve_network <- function(names, canopy, visitors, road_dist, peatland, threat_threshold = 0.75)
  1. Defensive Check:
    • Ensure that all five input vectors have the exact same length. If not, halt with stop("All parallel input vectors must be of identical length.").
  2. Iterative Evaluation:
    • Pre-allocate a numeric vector vulnerability_scores of length equal to length(names).
    • Pre-allocate a character vector action_plan of the same length.
    • Using a for loop over seq_along(names):
      • Call calculate_patch_vulnerability() for the $i$-th site.
      • Store the result in vulnerability_scores[i].
      • Using conditional branching (if / else):
        • If vulnerability_scores[i] >= threat_threshold, assign "Urgent Weed Eradication" to action_plan[i].
        • If vulnerability_scores[i] >= 0.40, assign "Routine Monitoring" to action_plan[i].
        • Otherwise, assign "Low Priority" to action_plan[i].
  3. Assemble Summary Data Frame:
    • Construct and return a data frame with columns:
      • "reserve"
      • "vulnerability"
      • "action"
      • "high_risk" (a logical column where vulnerability >= threat_threshold)

Run the audit on the 6 protected reserves:

reserve_audit <- audit_reserve_network(
  names            = reserve_names,
  canopy           = canopy_cover,
  visitors         = visitor_density,
  road_dist        = road_dist_km,
  peatland         = is_peatland,
  threat_threshold = 0.75
)

reserve_audit

Examine the output data frame. How did the peatland soil modifier affect the vulnerability score of Cairn_Moss relative to Dune_Reach?

docs.title: Practical 4 - Randomness, Sampling, and Stochastic Simulation
Introduction
docs.text:
In Practicals 1 to 3, all your calculations were deterministic: given the same inputs, your code produced the exact same outputs every single time.

In nature, however, ecological and environmental processes are inherently stochastic. Ecological surveys capture random samples from wider populations; individual organisms face probabilistic risks of mortality, predation, or disease; and environmental drivers fluctuate unpredictably.

Textbooks often treat probability as a collection of abstract formulas. In computational data science, however, the computer is an experimental laboratory where you can observe, manipulate, and experience randomness firsthand. In this practical, you will learn to:

  1. Generate pseudo-random variates using continuous distributions (runif, rnorm) and discrete sampling (sample, sample.int).
  2. Control simulation reproducibility using random number seeds (set.seed).
  3. Model probabilistic events across entire vectors without loops (e.g., survival, detection, extirpation).
  4. Build intuition for rare events and waiting times: how many trials does it actually take for an event with probability 0.05 to occur?
  5. Physically experience the difference between an expectation value and a sample mean: using an R closure to reveal the invisible attractor of an unknown, loaded process.
  6. Compare visual representations of probability: frequency histograms versus Empirical Cumulative Distribution Functions (ecdf).

docs.title: Generating Random Variates in R
docs.text: R includes built-in pseudo-random number generators for all standard probability distributions. By convention, random number generating functions begin with the letter r (for random).

docs.title: Continuous Uniform Distribution: runif()
docs.text:
The uniform distribution models situations where any real number within a given interval [min, max] is equally likely to be selected:

runif(n, min = 0, max = 1)
  • n: Number of random numbers to generate.
  • min: Lower limit (defaults to 0).
  • max: Upper limit (defaults to 1).
# Simulate 5 random microclimate humidity fractions between 0.30 and 0.85:
runif(n = 5, min = 0.30, max = 0.85)

If you omit min and max, R defaults to drawing numbers uniformly from the unit interval [0, 1].

docs.title: Continuous Normal Distribution: rnorm()
docs.text:
The normal (Gaussian) distribution produces a bell-shaped curve centered around a specified mean, with spread controlled by its standard deviation:

rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  • n: Number of random observations.
  • mean: Central expectation (defaults to 0).
  • sd: Standard deviation, defining spread (defaults to 1; must be non-negative).
# Simulate adult body lengths (cm) for 6 individual trout (mean = 28.5 cm, sd = 3.2 cm):
rnorm(n = 6, mean = 28.5, sd = 3.2)

docs.title: Discrete Sampling and Random Permutations: sample() and sample.int()
docs.text:
To pick elements randomly from a discrete set or vector, use sample():

sample(x, size, replace = FALSE, prob = NULL)
  • x: A vector of elements from which to choose.
  • size: Number of items to pick.
  • replace: A logical scalar. If FALSE (the default), elements are drawn without replacement (each item can be selected at most once). If TRUE, elements are drawn with replacement (the same item can be picked multiple times).
  • prob: Optional vector of probability weights if elements are not equally likely.
# Simulate drawing 4 tree counts from discrete values between 5 and 20 WITH replacement:
sample(x = 5:20, size = 4, replace = TRUE)

# Randomly select 3 field plots from 10 candidate sites WITHOUT replacement:
site_ids <- paste0("Site_", 1:10)
sample(x = site_ids, size = 3, replace = FALSE)

If you only need to sample integers from 1 to n, the optimized function sample.int(n, size, ...) is faster and concise:

# Pick a single random integer between 1 and 100:
random_station <- sample.int(100, size = 1)
random_station

docs.title: Reproducibility and the Random Seed: set.seed()
docs.text:
Computers cannot produce genuinely random numbers; they use deterministic mathematical algorithms (pseudo-random number generators) that start from an initial number called a seed.

If you do not specify a seed, R initializes its generator from your computer's system clock, giving different numbers on every run. When writing reproducible reports, testing scripts, or preparing unit tests, you can fix the seed using set.seed():

set.seed(42)
runif(3)
# [1] 0.9148060 0.9370754 0.2861395

# Running it again produces different numbers:
runif(3)
# [1] 0.8304476 0.6417455 0.5190959

# Resetting the seed reproduces the exact sequence:
set.seed(42)
runif(3)
# [1] 0.9148060 0.9370754 0.2861395

Rule for Simulations: Use set.seed() at the top of your final script when you need identical, reproducible output for an assessment or publication. During exploratory testing, run without a fixed seed to confirm your code behaves properly across different random realizations.

docs.title: Q1. Practice with Random Generators
docs.text:
1. Write an expression to generate 15 random numbers drawn uniformly between 10.0 and 50.0.
  2. Write an expression that samples 5 whole numbers between 1 and 50 without replacement. What happens if you request size = 60 with replace = FALSE?
  3. Generate 8 values from a normal distribution with mean = 100 and sd = 15.

docs.title: Simulating Random Events with Vectorized Expressions
docs.text: In ecological models, we frequently need to decide whether a discrete event occurs for each member of a population (e.g., does an individual disperse? does a seed germinate? does a patch experience extirpation?).

docs.title: The Uniform Threshold Technique
docs.text:
To simulate an event that occurs with probability p (where 0 <= p <= 1), compare a uniform random number in [0, 1] against p:

Event occurs if: runif(1) < p

Because runif(1) is distributed evenly between 0 and 1, the probability that it falls below p is exactly p.

Crucially, because relational operators (<, <=) are fully vectorized in R, you can simulate thousands of independent events simultaneously without writing a single loop:

# Suppose we have 8 habitat patches, each with an annual extirpation risk of 0.20:
n_patches <- 8
p_extirpation <- 0.20

# Draw 8 random values:
random_draws <- runif(n_patches)

# Vectorized event check:
went_extinct <- random_draws < p_extirpation
went_extinct
# [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE

docs.title: Heterogeneous Probabilities Across Individuals
docs.text:
This vectorized pattern works equally well when each individual or patch has its own unique risk probability:

# 5 individual fish, each with a different predation risk based on body size:
predation_risk <- c(0.10, 0.45, 0.05, 0.80, 0.30)

# Simulate predation events in a single vectorized step:
eaten <- runif(length(predation_risk)) < predation_risk
eaten

docs.title: Q2. Vectorized Survival
docs.text: A population of 100 seeds is planted in a restoration project. Each seed has an independent germination probability of 0.65. 1. Using a single vectorized expression (no loops), generate a logical vector of length 100 indicating which seeds germinated. 2. How many seeds in your simulation germinated? (Hint: sum() counts TRUE entries).

docs.title: Experiencing Randomness
docs.text:
Probabilistic intuition is notoriously deceiving. We tend to expect random processes to look neatly structured or evenly spread out, and we underestimate how much natural clumpiness, streaking, and fluctuation occurs purely by chance.

Let us explore four fundamental phenomena through direct computational experimentation.

docs.title: 1. The Waiting Game: How Long Until Something with p = 0.05 Happens?
docs.text:
In experimental science and statistical hypothesis testing, an event with probability p = 0.05 is often considered "rare" (occurring on average 1 in 20 times).

Does this mean that if you run trials, the event will reliably occur around trial 20? Let us find out.

We will write a while loop that counts how many independent trials it takes until a rare event (p = 0.05) occurs for the first time:

trial_count <- 0
event_occurred <- FALSE

while (!event_occurred) {
  trial_count <- trial_count + 1
  # Test if event occurs on this trial:
  if (runif(1) < 0.05) {
    event_occurred <- TRUE
  }
}

cat("Event occurred on trial number:", trial_count, "\n")

Run that code block in your console 5 to 10 times in succession. Notice the dramatic unpredictability: * In one run, the event might strike on trial 2 or 3. * In another run, you might wait 45, 60, or even more than 100 trials without seeing it occur.

docs.title: Repeated Simulation: The Waiting-Time Distribution
docs.text:
To see the full pattern, let us automate this experiment across 1,000 independent simulated runs:

simulate_waiting_time <- function(p = 0.05) {
  steps <- 0
  while (TRUE) {
    steps <- steps + 1
    if (runif(1) < p) {
      return(steps)
    }
  }
}

# Run 1000 independent replications:
n_reps <- 1000
waiting_times <- rep(NA, n_reps)

for (i in seq_len(n_reps)) {
  waiting_times[i] <- simulate_waiting_time(p = 0.05)
}

# Plot waiting times across all 1000 successive runs:
plot(waiting_times, pch = 16, col = "grey50",
     xlab = "Simulation Run", ylab = "Trials Until First Event",
     main = "Waiting Times Across 1000 Independent Realizations")
abline(h = 20, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)  # Theoretical average wait (1 / 0.05)
legend("topright", legend = "Expected Mean (20 trials)", col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

Look at the plot: * Each point represents one complete simulation run. Notice the dense cloud of points hugging the bottom axis: in a large proportion of runs, the event occurred within the first 5 to 15 trials. * More than half of the runs finish below the theoretical average wait of 20 trials (the red dashed line). * At the same time, look at the erratic spikes shooting high above the average: occasionally, you wait 60, 80, or even more than 100 trials!

Now, let us group these 1,000 individual runs into a frequency histogram to view the aggregated distribution:

# Visualise the distribution of waiting times:
hist(waiting_times, breaks = 30, col = "skyblue", 
     xlab = "Number of trials until first event",
     main = "Waiting Times for an Event with p = 0.05")
abline(v = mean(waiting_times), col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", legend = paste("Mean =", round(mean(waiting_times), 1)), 
       col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

Takeaway: Randomness exhibits geometric waiting times. Even when the expected average wait is 20 trials, waiting times are heavily skewed. Long runs without an event are common and natural, not evidence of a broken system.

docs.title: 2. Expectation vs. Mean: Discovering the Invisible Attractor of an Unknown System
docs.text:
In introductory textbooks, probability and expectation are often presented using symmetrical objects like fair coins or fair dice. But this makes the concept of expectation deceptively trivial: if a die has faces 1 through 6, people simply calculate the arithmetic average (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 3.5 and assume that is all there is to it.

In real nature, however, there are no symmetric dice. * Organisms do not have equal probabilities of surviving or dying. * Seeds do not have equal chances of dispersing to every location. * We never know the underlying probabilities in advance.

Furthermore, defining probability and expectation in words quickly leads to circular reasoning: we define probability as the expected relative frequency over infinite trials, and we define expectation as the probability-weighted sum of outcomes. You cannot define either word without already relying on the other!

The only way to break out of this circle and understand what an expectation value truly is—and how it fundamentally differs from a sample mean—is to experience it computationally on an unknown, loaded system.

docs.title: Building a "Mystery Loaded Die" using an R Closure
docs.text:
In R, a closure is a function that carries its own private, enclosed environment. Variables stored inside a closure remain sealed away from your global workspace: you cannot see them in your RStudio Environment panel, and you cannot accidentally tamper with them.

We can use a closure to create a unique "mystery die" for each student. Run the following code to define the generator factory:

create_mystery_die <- function(student_id) {
  # Save current RNG state so this setup does not alter global randomness:
  old_seed <- if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)) get(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv) else NULL

  # Initialize secret, non-uniform probabilities based on the student's ID:
  set.seed(student_id)
  weights <- runif(6, min = 0.2, max = 2.5)
  secret_probs <- weights / sum(weights)
  secret_expectation <- sum((1:6) * secret_probs)

  # Restore the prior global RNG state:
  if (!is.null(old_seed)) assign(".Random.seed", old_seed, envir = .GlobalEnv)

  # Return the rolling function (closure) containing the sealed probabilities:
  function(n = 1, reveal = FALSE) {
    if (reveal) {
      return(list(probabilities = round(secret_probs, 4), 
                  expectation   = round(secret_expectation, 4)))
    }
    sample(1:6, size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = secret_probs)
  }
}

Now, instantiate your personal die by supplying your student ID number (or any unique integer of your choice):

# Replace 12345 with your actual student ID number:
my_die <- create_mystery_die(student_id = 12345)

Look at your RStudio Environment panel. my_die is simply listed as a function. The underlying probabilities are locked inside.

Roll your mystery die a few times:

my_die(1)   # Roll once
my_die(10)  # Roll 10 times

docs.title: The Noisy Sample Mean
docs.text:
What is the "average" outcome of your die? Because the die is loaded with secret weights, you cannot calculate (1 + ... + 6) / 6.

Let us compute the sample mean across a small sample of 15 rolls:

mean(my_die(15))

Run that line three or four times in your console. Notice how erratic the result is: * In one run, you might get 4.2. * In the next, you might get 2.8. * In another, 3.5.

The sample mean (mean(x)) is an empirical calculation from real, collected data. It is noisy, erratic, and changes on every single survey. If you were a field ecologist with a small sample size (n = 15), you would have no idea what the true underlying property of this system actually is.

docs.title: Watching Multiple Parallel Universes Converge
docs.text:
If the expectation value cannot be reliably observed in a single sample, how does it physically manifest?

Let us simulate rolling your mystery die 2,000 times. But instead of watching just one sequence, let us simulate 5 independent parallel universes running side by side, and plot their running sample means as data accumulates:

n_rolls <- 2000
n_universes <- 5

# Set up an empty coordinate space:
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, n_rolls), ylim = c(1.5, 5.5),
     xlab = "Number of Die Rolls (Sample Size n)",
     ylab = "Cumulative Running Mean",
     main = "5 Independent Realizations of Your Mystery Die")

# Assign distinct colours to each parallel history:
palette <- c("steelblue", "forestgreen", "darkorange", "purple", "firebrick")

# Pre-allocate a vector to record the final asymptotic estimates:
final_estimates <- numeric(n_universes)

# Simulate and overlay each running trajectory:
for (k in seq_len(n_universes)) {
  rolls <- my_die(n = n_rolls)
  running_mean <- cumsum(rolls) / seq_len(n_rolls)
  lines(running_mean, col = palette[k], lwd = 1.4)
  final_estimates[k] <- running_mean[n_rolls]
}

Examine this plot carefully. It captures the physical essence of what statisticians call the Law of Large Numbers:

  1. The Early Fan of Chaos (n < 50): Look at the left edge of the plot. Each universe lives in its own wild reality. In one universe, early high rolls push the running mean up; in another, early low rolls drag it down. If you stopped sampling here, you would conclude that the universes follow completely different laws of nature.
  2. The Inevitable Collapse into the Center of Gravity (n > 500): Now follow the lines to the right as n crosses 500, 1,000, and 2,000 rolls. None of these five simulations have any awareness of each other. The random number generator does not "remember" past rolls to balance out bad luck. Yet, despite being completely independent and random, all five lines are inexorably funneled into the exact same horizontal asymptote.
  3. Compare with Your Neighbour: Look at the screen of the student sitting next to you. Their five lines also converged into a razor-thin horizontal beam—but their beam converged at a completely different number from yours!

docs.title: Revealing the Secret Expectation
docs.text:
Estimate where your five parallel histories converged by averaging their final endpoints:

cat("Empirical estimate of the attractor:", round(mean(final_estimates), 3), "\n")

Now, unlock the closure and reveal the true mathematical properties baked into your die:

truth <- my_die(reveal = TRUE)
truth

Overlay this true expectation onto your plot as a dashed black line:

abline(h = truth$expectation, col = "black", lty = 2, lwd = 2.5)
legend("topright", 
       legend = c("Independent Sample Histories", paste("True Expectation =", truth$expectation)),
       col = c("steelblue", "black"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = c(1.4, 2.5))

Look at how the dashed line cuts directly through the convergence channel.

Reflect deeply on what you have just witnessed: * The sample mean is an empirical measurement. It lives in the data. It is noisy and changes with every sample. * The expectation value is not an average of data. It was fixed the moment create_mystery_die was executed—before a single die was ever rolled. * The expectation value is the invisible center of gravity of the generating mechanism. The Law of Large Numbers is the physical guarantee that as individual random observations accumulate, their collective historical average is inexorably captured by this invisible attractor.

docs.title: Zooming In: The Small-Sample Trap
docs.text:
To understand why field biology and conservation surveys are so difficult, zoom into the first 100 rolls of your experiment:

# Re-plot focusing strictly on small sample sizes (n = 1 to 100):
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 100), ylim = c(1.5, 5.5),
     xlab = "Number of Die Rolls (Sample Size n)",
     ylab = "Cumulative Running Mean",
     main = "The Small-Sample Trap: First 100 Rolls")
abline(h = truth$expectation, col = "black", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

for (k in seq_len(n_universes)) {
  rolls <- my_die(n = 100)
  running_mean <- cumsum(rolls) / seq_len(100)
  lines(running_mean, col = palette[k], lwd = 1.4)
}

Notice how wide the spread remains even at n = 50. When researchers report "the average body mass is 3.2 kg" from a field survey of 30 animals, they often assume their sample mean accurately reflects the underlying expectation. As your plot demonstrates, that intuition is frequently overconfident.

docs.title: Q3. Testing the Attractor of a Continuous Uniform Distribution
docs.text: If a variable is drawn uniformly from continuous values between 10.0 and 20.0 (runif(n, min = 10.0, max = 20.0)), every real value in that interval is equally likely. 1. What is the theoretical expectation (center of gravity) of this continuous distribution? 2. Write a script that simulates 4 independent histories of 1,500 uniform draws between 10.0 and 20.0, and plots their running means simultaneously on a single graph. 3. Overlay a horizontal dashed line at the theoretical expectation. At approximately what sample size n do all 4 independent histories consistently stay within +/- 0.2 of the expectation?

docs.title: 3. Variance, Standard Deviation, and the 1 / sqrt(n) Convergence Rule
docs.text:
While the sample mean converges to the true expectation, individual observations do not become less variable.

Let us generate samples of varying sizes from a standard normal distribution (mean = 0, sd = 1):

sample_small <- rnorm(20, mean = 0, sd = 1)
sample_large <- rnorm(5000, mean = 0, sd = 1)

sd(sample_small)  # Might be 0.82 or 1.18 (noisy estimate)
sd(sample_large)  # Very close to 1.00

Notice the crucial difference: * Standard Deviation (s): Measures the spread of the underlying population. It remains approximately constant (~1.0) regardless of how many data points you collect. * Standard Error of the Mean (SE = s / sqrt(n)): Measures the uncertainty in the estimated mean. It shrinks proportionally to 1 / sqrt(n).

To cut your estimation uncertainty in half, you must collect four times as much data (2^2 = 4).

docs.title: 4. Histograms vs. Empirical Cumulative Distribution Functions (ECDF)
docs.text:
When visualizing continuous random data, researchers typically reach for a histogram. However, histograms have a serious drawback: their visual shape is sensitive to arbitrary bin boundaries.

A complementary tool is the Empirical Cumulative Distribution Function (ECDF). The ECDF at any point x shows the exact fraction of observations in the data that are less than or equal to x:

F_n(x) = (Number of observations <= x) / n

Let us compare both views on a sample of 200 normal variates:

set.seed(101)
sim_data <- rnorm(200, mean = 15.0, sd = 3.0)

# Set up side-by-side plot layout:
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

# 1. Frequency Histogram:
hist(sim_data, breaks = 15, col = "lightgrey", 
     main = "Histogram (Binned Density)", xlab = "Measured Value")

# 2. Empirical Cumulative Distribution Function:
plot(ecdf(sim_data), verticals = TRUE, col = "navy",
     main = "Empirical Cumulative Distribution",
     xlab = "Measured Value", ylab = "Cumulative Proportion <= x")
abline(h = 0.5, col = "red", lty = 3)  # Marks the 50th percentile (median)
abline(v = 15.0, col = "red", lty = 3)

# Reset plotting layout to single panel:
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Reading the ECDF: * Look at the y-axis: the curve rises smoothly from 0.0 (minimum value) to 1.0 (maximum value). * At the median (x ~ 15.0), exactly half of the cumulative probability (y = 0.50) has accumulated. * Steep sections in the ECDF indicate regions where data points are densely clustered; flat sections indicate sparse regions.

docs.title: Q4. Inspecting the ECDF
docs.text: Using sim_data from above: 1. Use mean(sim_data <= 12.0) to calculate the exact proportion of data points that are <= 12.0. 2. Verify where this point falls on the vertical axis of your ECDF plot.

docs.title: Practical Review Exercises
docs.text: Work through these multi-step exercises in your R script. Focus on combining your custom functions, loop structures, and vectorized operations with the stochastic tools introduced today.

docs.title: Exercise 1: The Mark-Release-Recapture Lincoln-Petersen Simulator
docs.text:
In wildlife biology, ecologists estimate the size of an elusive animal population (N_true) using the Lincoln-Petersen mark-recapture method:

  1. In the first sampling session, M animals are captured, marked, and released back into the wild.
  2. After allowing time for marked animals to mix into the population, a second sample of C animals is captured.
  3. The number of marked individuals recaptured in the second sample is recorded as R.
  4. The estimated total population size (N_hat) is calculated as: 
    N_hat = (M * C) / R

Because recapture is a stochastic process, R fluctuates randomly across surveys, causing N_hat to vary.

docs.title: Part A: Simulating a Single Recapture Survey
docs.text:
Write a function named simulate_recapture_survey with the signature:

simulate_recapture_survey <- function(n_true, m_marked, c_captured) {
  # Your code here
}

The function must execute these steps:

  1. Defensive Validation:
    • Verify that n_true, m_marked, and c_captured are single numeric integers >= 1.
    • Verify that m_marked <= n_true and c_captured <= n_true. If violated, halt with stop().
  2. Population Representation:
    • Represent the population of size n_true as an integer vector: marked individuals are represented by 1, and unmarked individuals by 0.
    • Construct this vector using rep(): 
      population <- c(rep(1, m_marked), rep(0, n_true - m_marked))
  3. Simulating Capture:
    • Draw a sample of size c_captured from population without replacement using sample().
    • Count how many marked individuals were recaptured by summing the sample (R).
  4. Estimation:
    • If R > 0, compute N_hat = (M * C) / R.
    • If R == 0 (no marked animals were recaptured), the formula divides by zero; return NA.
  5. Return N_hat as a single numeric scalar.

Test your function with a known population:

simulate_recapture_survey(n_true = 500, m_marked = 80, c_captured = 60)

Run this line three or four times. Notice that even though the true population is fixed at 500, the estimate fluctuates.

docs.title: Part B: Evaluating Estimator Bias and Variance
docs.text:
Now, write an iterated simulation script to evaluate how well the Lincoln-Petersen estimator performs:

  1. Fix the parameters: n_true = 1000, m_marked = 150, and c_captured = 100.
  2. Pre-allocate a numeric vector named pop_estimates of length 500.
  3. Using a for loop, run simulate_recapture_survey() 500 times, storing each returned estimate in pop_estimates.
  4. Calculate the proportion of surveys that failed due to zero recaptures (mean(is.na(pop_estimates))).
  5. Compute the average population estimate across all valid surveys (mean(pop_estimates, na.rm = TRUE)). How close is this to the true value of 1,000?
  6. Plot a histogram of the valid estimates and overlay a vertical red line marking the true population size (1000).

docs.title: Exercise 2: Forest Gap Disturbance & Tree Recruitment Dynamics
docs.text:
In temperate rainforests, canopy trees persist for centuries until catastrophic windthrow storms create light gaps, triggering new sapling recruitment.

We will simulate a stand of 100 canopy trees over annual time steps.

docs.title: Problem Formulation
docs.text:
• Stand State: The stand is represented by a numeric vector tree_ages of length 100, where each element is the age of the tree occupying that canopy position.
  • Annual Disturbance Risk: In any given year, an extreme windstorm occurs with probability p_storm = 0.08.
  • Tree Mortality:
    • If a windstorm occurs in year t, older trees are vulnerable to windthrow: any tree with age > 60 years suffers an 80% mortality rate (each older tree dies independently with probability 0.80).
    • Younger trees (age <= 60) have flexible trunks and survive the storm.
    • In years without a storm, trees simply age by 1 year.
  • Gap Regeneration: When a tree dies, its position is immediately colonized by a new seedling of age = 1 year.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Write a function named simulate_forest_year that updates the stand across a single annual time step: 

    simulate_forest_year <- function(tree_ages, p_storm = 0.08) {
  # Your code here
}

    • Validate that tree_ages is a numeric vector with length >= 1 and contains no negative values.
    • Check if a storm occurs this year by testing runif(1) < p_storm.
    • If a storm occurs:
      • Identify indices of vulnerable trees where tree_ages > 60.
      • For each vulnerable tree, determine if it dies using vectorized random uniform numbers: runif(n_vulnerable) < 0.80.
      • Reset the age of trees that died to 1.
      • For all trees that survived, increase their age by 1.
    • If no storm occurs:
      • Increment the age of all trees by 1.
    • Return the updated tree_ages vector.

  2. Write a multi-year simulation function named run_forest_simulation: 

    run_forest_simulation <- function(initial_ages, n_years, p_storm = 0.08) {
  # Your code here
}

    • Pre-allocate a numeric vector named mean_age_trajectory of length n_years + 1.
    • Record the initial mean stand age in mean_age_trajectory[1].
    • Using a for loop over 1:n_years, iteratively update the forest stand and record the mean tree age at each step.
    • Return a named list containing:
      • final_stand: The vector of tree ages at the end of the simulation.
      • mean_ages: The annual trajectory of mean stand age.

  3. Run a 150-year simulation starting from an even-aged mature stand: 

    set.seed(456)
initial_stand <- rep(50, 100) # 100 trees, all 50 years old

sim_results <- run_forest_simulation(initial_ages = initial_stand, n_years = 150, p_storm = 0.08)

# Plot mean stand age trajectory over time:
plot(sim_results$mean_ages, type = "l", col = "forestgreen", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Year", ylab = "Mean Canopy Age (years)",
     main = "Forest Stand Age Under Stochastic Storm Disturbance")

Examine the trajectory plot. Why does the mean age show gradual upward climbs punctuated by sudden sharp drops?

docs.title: Exercise 3: Empirical Quantiles and the 5% Rare Event Risk
docs.text:
In environmental management, the "1-in-20 year" flood or storm corresponds to an annual exceedance probability of p = 0.05.

When planning infrastructure or conservation reserves, stakeholders often mistakenly assume that a 1-in-20 year event will happen roughly once every 20 years. In reality, multiple rare events can strike in quick succession, or a site may experience decades of calm.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Write a function named sample_events_in_horizon that simulates the total number of rare events observed over a 20-year operational planning horizon: 

    sample_events_in_horizon <- function(horizon_years = 20, p_annual = 0.05) {
  # Draw horizon_years uniform numbers and count how many are < p_annual
  event_count <- sum(runif(horizon_years) < p_annual)
  return(event_count)
}

  2. Run an iterated simulation:

    • Execute sample_events_in_horizon() 2,000 times.
    • Store the resulting counts in a numeric vector named observed_counts.

  3. Analyze the empirical risk profile across the 2,000 simulated 20-year horizons:

    • What proportion of 20-year periods experienced exactly zero rare events? (mean(observed_counts == 0))
    • What proportion experienced two or more rare events? (mean(observed_counts >= 2))
    • What was the maximum number of rare events observed in a single 20-year window?

  4. Plot a bar plot or frequency histogram of observed_counts: 

    counts_table <- table(observed_counts) / length(observed_counts)
barplot(counts_table, col = "salmon",
        xlab = "Number of Events Experienced in 20 Years",
        ylab = "Empirical Probability",
        main = "Realised Frequency of a '1-in-20 Year' (p = 0.05) Event")

Reflect on your findings: over a 20-year window, are you more likely to experience zero events, or at least one event? How does this computational experiment change your interpretation of a "1-in-20 year" risk?

docs.title: Practical 1 - Introduction to RStudio, Basic Data Types, and Vectors
Introduction
docs.text:
This practical series teaches core computational programming in R, focusing on the concepts required for computational modelling, data manipulation, and scientific workflows.

The practicals move quickly. You will need to engage actively with the concepts, experiment in your script editor, and complete the exercises to build the technical foundation required for the assessment challenges. Make full use of R's built-in help system, discuss problems with your neighbour, and call over a demonstrator if you need clarification.

docs.title: The RStudio Environment
docs.text:
Open RStudio on your computer.

RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE)—a front-end interface that makes working with R intuitive and productive. R itself is the underlying engine doing all the actual work in the background.

Acquaint yourself with the four primary panels in RStudio:

+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
|                                    |                                    |
|         Source / Script Editor     |          Environment / History     |
|          (Top Left)                |           (Top Right)              |
|                                    |                                    |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+
|                                    |                                    |
|         Console / Terminal         |          Files / Plots / Help      |
|          (Bottom Left)             |           (Bottom Right)           |
|                                    |                                    |
+------------------------------------+------------------------------------+

docs.title: The Console
docs.text:
• In the bottom-left panel, find the tab called Console. You can type commands here for immediate execution. Type 1 + 2 and press Enter (or Return). As output, you will see: 

    [1] 3
    The [1] indicates that the display line begins with the 1st element of the returned vector (which here contains a single value). The 3 is the computed result.

  • Continuing in the Console, type: 

    a <- 7 - 2
    and press Enter. The answer is not printed to the console. Look at the Environment tab in the top-right panel: it now lists a with its assigned value 5.

  • You can inspect the value of a by typing a into the console and pressing Enter. R evaluates the symbol and prints [1] 5.

  • In the Console, you can cycle through previously entered commands using the Up and Down arrow keys on your keyboard.

Important: While the Console is useful for quick calculations, scientific programming must be reproducible. Never rely on commands typed directly into the Console for your permanent work. All code, data pipelines, and calculations should be written into script files.

docs.title: The R Script Editor
docs.text:
We will write all permanent commands into an R script file and execute them from the editor.

  • In the menu bar, click File -> New File -> R Script (or use Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows/Linux, Cmd+Shift+N on macOS). A blank editor tab will appear in the top-left panel.

  • Type a mathematical expression: 

    2 * a + 8
    Press Enter. A new line opens, but nothing is calculated yet: we have not instructed R to evaluate the line.

  • Place your cursor anywhere on the line with 2 * a + 8 and press Ctrl+Enter (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Enter (macOS). The line is automatically sent to the Console below and evaluated.

  • In your script, type: 

    a <- a + 1000
    Press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter). Observe how the value associated with a in the Environment tab updates immediately.

  • You can run multiple lines or an entire script at once. Select several lines, or even just parts of lines, with your mouse (or press Ctrl+A / Cmd+A to highlight the entire script), then press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter).

  • To save your script, click File -> Save (Ctrl+S / Cmd+S). Choose an informative filename. RStudio will automatically append the .R file extension.

docs.title: The Help System
docs.text:
The Help tab in the bottom-right panel is an essential resource.

  • In your script editor or console, type sum and place the text cursor within the word. Press F1. The documentation for sum will open in the Help tab. Alternatively, run: 

    ?sum

  • Help pages follow a consistent structure. When learning a new function, read the sections in this recommended order:

  • Description: A concise summary of what the function accomplishes.
  • Usage & Arguments: The parameters the function expects, their default values, and the expected input structure. Then skip down to...
  • Value: What the function returns (a scalar number, a vector, a list, etc.).

  • Examples: Working code snippets at the bottom of the page that you can paste into your script and run.

  • If you do not know the exact name of a function, use a double question mark to search across all installed packages: 

    ??logarithm

docs.title: Q1. Using the Help page for sum:
docs.text: Find out how to compute the sum of all integers from 1 to 100 using R's sequence operator :.

docs.title: Good Coding Practice
docs.text: Writing readable, well-structured code is just as vital as writing code that runs. In professional computational science, code is read far more often than it is written. Clean layouts reduce the likelyhood of errors and ensure that collaborators and assessors can follow your analytical logic.

docs.title: White Space, Indentation, and Comments
docs.text:
• Comments: Any text following a # character is ignored by R until the end of the line. Try to use comments to summarise to what end a calculation is performed, rather than merely restating the code.
  • White Space: Spaces around operators (+, -, *, <-, ==) and after commas make code legible. Compare x<-3*y+2 with x <- 3 * y + 2.
  • Descriptive Names: Avoid single-letter variables except for temporary indexing counters. A variable named canopy_cover conveys intent; a variable named cc or x invites errors.
  • Consistency: Stick to snake case (my_variable_name) for variable and function names.

Consider the contrast between these two scripts performing identical calculations:

docs.title: Bad Practice:
docs.text:
boooom <-0.01
blah2          =0.005
    blah3<- 0.0036
bigblah                           = boooom+ blah2        + blah3
tadayeahmanfunky<-100*exp(bigblah*10)
tadayeahmanfunky

docs.title: Good Practice:
docs.text:
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Program:     bacterial_growth.R
# Purpose:     Calculates projected population size under exponential growth.
# Inputs:      Nutrient availability, temperature anomaly, relative humidity.
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Define environmental input parameters
nutrients   <- 0.01    # Proportional nutrient supplementation
temperature <- 0.005   # Degrees C deviation from 20 C baseline
humidity    <- 0.0036  # Proportional humidity index

# Define initial culture parameters
starting_cells <- 100  # Initial cell count
incubation_hrs <- 10   # Duration in hours

# Calculate compound growth rate
growth_rate <- nutrients + temperature + humidity

# Project final population size: N(t) = N_0 * exp(r * t)
final_cells <- starting_cells * exp(growth_rate * incubation_hrs)

# Display final cell count
final_cells

docs.title: Q2. In your script editor, write a clean, well-commented script that calculates the volume and total surface area of a rectangular storage container:
docs.text:
• Length = 6.5m
  • Width = 3.2m
  • Height = 2.4m

Store each dimension in a descriptively named variable. Compute the volume (L x W x H) and total surface area (2 x [LW + LH + WH]), save them in separate variables, and print both results to the console.

docs.title: Variables and Assignment
docs.text:
A variable stores a value or an object in computer memory under a designated name. In R, assignment is performed using the arrow operator <-, typed as a less-than sign and a hyphen (please copy and execute commands in boxes for later use of results; also make sure you understand each line of code; feel free to play with the code to see what happens):

dissolved_oxygen_mg_l <- 8.45
sensor_depth_m        <- 12.0

Always use <- for assignment. Although R permits the equals sign = for assignment, = is reserved by convention for setting function arguments inside function calls (e.g., seq(from = 1, to = 10)).

Rules for variable names in R:

  • Names can contain letters, numbers, underscores (_), and periods (.). Using underscores (snake_case) is standard practice.
  • Names must start with a letter (or a period not immediately followed by a number).
  • Names cannot contain spaces or arithmetic operators (-, +, *, /).
  • R is strictly case-sensitive: Water_Temp, water_temp, and WATER_TEMP refer to three completely different variables.

docs.title: Data Classes and Types
docs.text:
Every piece of data stored in R belongs to an underlying class that dictates how R executes operations on it. The core atomic data types are:

  1. Numeric (Double): Real numbers with decimal precision (e.g., 3.1415, -0.5, 42).
  2. Integer: Whole numbers (e.g., 5L, 12L). In R, numbers entered without a decimal point are still stored as doubles by default unless explicitly followed by L or converted via as.integer().
  3. Character: Text strings enclosed in matching single or double quotation marks (e.g., 'Salmo trutta', "Transect_A").
  4. Logical: Boolean truth values: TRUE or FALSE (unquoted, uppercase).

You can check the class of any variable using class(). Set

station_id      <- "Station_North_4"
water_salinity  <- 34.8
replicate_count <- 4L
sensor_active   <- TRUE

Now try

class(station_id)       
class(water_salinity)   
class(replicate_count)  
class(sensor_active)

docs.title: Type Checking and Explicit Conversion
docs.text:
In computational pipelines and data ingestion scripts, code must often verify that inputs conform to expected types. R provides a family of is.*() functions to verify types, and as.*() functions to coerce between types:

Type Check Conversion Function Example Behaviour is.numeric(x) as.numeric(x) "14.75" -> 14.75 is.integer(x) as.integer(x) 14.9 -> 14L (truncates decimal) is.character(x) as.character(x) 250 -> "250" is.logical(x) as.logical(x) 1 -> TRUE, 0 -> FALSE 
raw_reading <- "32.18"
is.numeric(raw_reading)      # FALSE (stored as character string)

clean_reading <- as.numeric(raw_reading)
is.numeric(clean_reading)    # TRUE

If you attempt to convert an incompatible character string to a number, R returns NA (Not Available) and issues a warning: 

as.numeric("invalid_sensor_signal")  # Returns NA with a warning

docs.title: Q3. What is the value and class of result after evaluating each of the following expressions? Predict the output before running the code in R:
docs.text:
• result <- as.integer(15.82)
  • result <- as.logical(0)
  • result <- as.character(FALSE)
  • result <- as.numeric("18.4") <= 20

docs.title: Logical Operators and Expressions
docs.text: A logical expression evaluates a condition and resolves to either TRUE or FALSE. Logical expressions are used, for example, for filtering data, testing for unusual conditions conditions ("edge cases"), and verifying input integrity.

docs.title: Relational Comparison Operators
docs.text:
• > : Greater than
  • < : Less than
  • >= : Greater than or equal to
  • <= : Less than or equal to
  • == : Exactly equal to (two equals signs; single = is assignment!)
  • != : Not equal to
turbidity_ntu <- 4.8

turbidity_ntu < 5.0   # TRUE
turbidity_ntu == 5.0  # FALSE
turbidity_ntu != 0.0  # TRUE

docs.title: Boolean Combination Operators
docs.text:
Individual logical tests can be combined using Boolean logic:

  • & : AND (evaluates to TRUE only if both conditions are TRUE).
  • | : OR (evaluates to TRUE if at least one condition is TRUE).
  • ! : NOT (inverts TRUE to FALSE, and FALSE to TRUE).
## Example use of logical variables
# Set paramters
dissolved_o2 <- 6.2
water_temp   <- 14.5

# Both conditions must hold:
hypoxia_risk <- (dissolved_o2 < 4.0) & (water_temp > 20.0)
hypoxia_risk  # FALSE

# At least one condition must hold:
suboptimal <- (dissolved_o2 < 5.0) | (water_temp > 18.0)
suboptimal    # FALSE

# Negation:
is_optimal <- !suboptimal
is_optimal    # TRUE

docs.title: Truth Table Summary:
docs.text:
• TRUE & TRUE -> TRUE
  • TRUE & FALSE -> FALSE
  • FALSE & FALSE -> FALSE
  • TRUE | FALSE -> TRUE
  • FALSE | FALSE -> FALSE
  • !TRUE -> FALSE

docs.title: Q4. Given a <- 18 and b <- 35, write logical expressions in R that test:
docs.text:
1. Whether a is strictly between 15 and 25 (exclusive of endpoints).
  2. Whether a is less than 10 or b is greater than or equal to 30.
  3. Whether b is divisible by 5 without a remainder (hint: use the modulo operator %%, where b %% 5 == 0 evaluates divisibility).

docs.title: Vectors: The Fundamental 1D Structure
docs.text:
A vector is an ordered collection of elements that must all belong to the same atomic class. If you attempt to combine items of different classes into a single vector, R silently converts them to the most flexible type (character is most flexible, followed by numeric, followed by logical).

Oddly, in R, an individual scalar such as x <- 5 is simply a vector of length 1.

docs.title: Creating Vectors
docs.text:
Construct vectors using c() (combine), sequence generators, or repeat functions:

# Direct combination:
conductivity_vals <- c(450, 520, 480, 610, 590)
site_labels       <- c("Estuary_1", "Estuary_2", "Estuary_3")
equipment_passed  <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)

# Sequences:
depth_profile <- seq(from = 0.0, to = 25.0, by = 5.0)  # 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25
station_ids   <- 101:108                               # Whole numbers 101 to 108
time_steps    <- seq(from = 0, to = 1, length.out = 5) # 5 evenly spaced values

# Repetitions:
baseline_zeros <- rep(0, times = 8)
treatment_tags <- rep(c("Ambient", "Enriched"), times = 3)
block_labels   <- rep(c("Zone_A", "Zone_B"), each = 4)

docs.title: Inspecting Vector Properties
docs.text:
• length(x): Total number of elements.
  • class(x): The atomic class of the elements.
  • head(x, n): First $n$ elements (defaults to 6).
  • tail(x, n): Last $n$ elements.
length(conductivity_vals)  # 5
class(conductivity_vals)   # "numeric"

docs.title: Q5. Generate a vector named temperature_steps that starts at 12.0, ends at 24.0, and contains exactly 25 evenly spaced values. What is the value of its 9th element?
Vectorized Arithmetic and Recycling
docs.text: In R, mathematical operations applied to vectors execute element-by-element without requiring loops. This vectorization makes operations computationally efficient and concise.

docs.title: Scalar-Vector Arithmetic
docs.text:
When an operation combines a vector with a single scalar, the scalar operation is applied to each element individually:

nitrate_ppm <- c(1.2, 2.5, 3.1, 0.8)

# Convert all measurements by adding a calibration offset of 0.3:
nitrate_ppm + 0.3          # 1.5 2.8 3.4 1.1

# Multiply each measurement by a conversion factor:
nitrate_ppm * 1000         # 1200 2500 3100  800

# Compute estimated ionic flux: flux = 1.5 * concentration + 0.2
nitrate_ppm * 1.5 + 0.2    # 2.00 3.95 4.85 1.40

docs.title: Vector-Vector Arithmetic and the Recycling Rule
docs.text:
When combining two vectors of identical length, arithmetic occurs pairwise:

flow_rates <- c(2.0, 3.5, 1.8)
widths     <- c(10.0, 12.0, 8.0)

# Pairwise product:
discharge <- flow_rates * widths
discharge  # 20.0 42.0 14.4

If two vectors differ in length, R recycles (repeats) the elements of the shorter vector until it matches the length of the longer vector:

sample_depths <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60)
adjustments   <- c(1, 2)

sample_depths + adjustments
# adjustments is recycled to c(1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2)
# Result: 11 22 31 42 51 62

Warning: If the length of the longer vector is not an exact integer multiple of the length of the shorter vector, R still executes the operation using partial recycling, but issues a warning message. In scientific scripts, this often indicates an accidental indexing or alignment mismatch.

docs.title: Q6. What does the following expression return?
docs.text:
c(2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) * c(1, -1)
Explain the recycling process that produced this output.

docs.title: Vector Subsetting and Indexing
docs.text:
Extracting and modifying specific subsets of a vector is a very common operation in R. We use square brackets [] for indexing.

There are four primary indexing mechanisms:

docs.title: 1. Positive Integer Indexing (Extraction)
docs.text:
Specify the 1-based index positions of the elements you wish to retrieve:

salinity <- c(31.2, 32.5, 34.1, 33.8, 30.9, 35.4)

salinity[1]          # First element: 31.2
salinity[4]          # Fourth element: 33.8
salinity[c(1, 3, 5)] # First, third, and fifth: 31.2 34.1 30.9
salinity[2:4]        # Elements 2 through 4: 32.5 34.1 33.8

docs.title: 2. Negative Integer Indexing (Exclusion)
docs.text:
Negative integers instruct R to omit the designated positions:

salinity[-1]         # Drops the first element
salinity[-c(2, 5)]   # Drops the 2nd and 5th elements

docs.title: 3. Logical Indexing (Filtering by Condition)
docs.text:
You can supply a logical vector of the same length inside the brackets. R retains only elements where the corresponding index entry is TRUE:

measurements <- c(12.5, 8.1, 19.4, 6.2, 14.8)
keep_mask    <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)
measurements[keep_mask]  # 12.5 19.4 14.8

Because relational comparisons generate logical vectors, conditions can be placed directly inside the brackets:

# Extract all salinity readings strictly greater than 33.0:
high_salinity <- salinity[salinity > 33.0]
high_salinity  # 34.1 33.8 35.4

# Extract salinity readings between 31.5 and 34.0:
mid_salinity <- salinity[salinity >= 31.5 & salinity <= 34.0]
mid_salinity   # 32.5 33.8

docs.title: 4. Named Indexing
docs.text:
Elements of a vector can have names assigned to them. You can extract elements using character names:

station_depths <- c(Stn_A = 14.5, Stn_B = 28.2, Stn_C = 8.7)
station_depths["Stn_B"]                # Returns 28.2
station_depths[c("Stn_A", "Stn_C")]   # Returns 14.5 8.7

docs.title: Modifying Vectors and In-Place Replacement
docs.text:
Indexing allows you to update or correct specific entries in place using assignment:

sensor_readings <- c(14.2, -999.0, 15.8, 16.1, -999.0, 14.9)

# Correct a single entry at index 2:
sensor_readings[2] <- 14.5

# Replace all error codes (-999.0) with NA:
sensor_readings[sensor_readings == -999.0] <- NA
sensor_readings

docs.title: Bounding and Clamping Values
docs.text:
Physical sensors or ecological rates often have theoretical operating boundaries. Values falling outside those boundaries can be clamped to valid limits using logical indexing:

photometer_absorbance <- c(-0.05, 0.42, 1.85, 2.15, 0.90, -0.01)

# Clamp lower boundary at 0.0 (no negative absorbance):
photometer_absorbance[photometer_absorbance < 0.0] <- 0.0

# Clamp upper boundary at 2.0 (detector saturation limit):
photometer_absorbance[photometer_absorbance > 2.0] <- 2.0

photometer_absorbance  # 0.00 0.42 1.85 2.00 0.90 0.00

docs.title: Q7. Given the a vector of this structure:
docs.text:
dissolved_co2 <- c(18.2, 24.5, 9.8, 31.0, 42.1, 14.3, 5.4, 28.7)
Write code to:

  1. Extract all concentrations that are strictly less than 12.0 or strictly greater than 30.0.
  2. Clamp the vector so that any value below 10.0 is set to 10.0, and any value exceeding 35.0 is set to 35.0.

docs.title: Missing Data (NA) and Vector Summaries
docs.text: In real-world field sampling and laboratory assays, measurements can be missing due to equipment downtime or uncollected samples. In R, missing entries are represented by the special constant NA (Not Available).

docs.title: Behaviour of NA
docs.text:
NA represents an unknown quantity. Standard arithmetic and relational comparisons involving NA yield NA:

10 + NA       # NA
NA > 5        # NA
NA == NA      # NA (you cannot test whether an unknown equals an unknown)

To test whether entries are missing, never use x == NA. Always use the dedicated function is.na():

chlorophyll_a <- c(2.4, NA, 3.8, 1.9, NA, 4.5)

is.na(chlorophyll_a)
# FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

# Count missing entries:
sum(is.na(chlorophyll_a))  # 2

# Extract only valid (non-missing) measurements:
valid_chlorophyll <- chlorophyll_a[!is.na(chlorophyll_a)]
valid_chlorophyll  # 2.4 3.8 1.9 4.5

docs.title: Vector Summaries and na.rm
docs.text:
Common aggregation functions across vectors include:

  • sum(): Sum of elements.
  • mean(): Arithmetic mean.
  • min(), max(): Extremes.
  • length(): Total length (including any NA entries).

If a vector contains missing data, summary functions return NA by default to warn you of incomplete data. To compute the summary over all available valid observations, supply the argument na.rm = TRUE:

mean(chlorophyll_a)                # NA
mean(chlorophyll_a, na.rm = TRUE)  # 3.15

docs.title: Logical Reductions: all(), any(), and which()
docs.text:
When checking input validity or data criteria across vectors:

  • any(condition): Returns TRUE if at least one element satisfies the condition.
  • all(condition): Returns TRUE only if every element satisfies the condition.
  • which(condition): Returns the integer indices where the condition evaluates to TRUE.
pressures_kpa <- c(101.3, 102.5, 98.4, 104.1, 99.2)

any(pressures_kpa < 100.0)    # TRUE
all(pressures_kpa > 90.0)     # TRUE
which(pressures_kpa > 102.0)  # 2 4 (2nd and 4th entries)

docs.title: Q8. You are given the following record of stream water temperatures:
docs.text:
stream_temps <- c(14.2, 16.5, NA, 15.1, 19.8, NA, 13.9, 17.0)
Write R expressions to:

  1. Check whether any recorded temperature exceeds 18.0C.
  2. Check whether all non-missing measurements are strictly above 12.0C.
  3. Compute the arithmetic mean of all non-missing temperatures.
  4. Replace all NA values in stream_temps with the baseline value 15.0C.

docs.title: Practical Review Exercises
docs.text: Work through these multi-step exercises in your R script. Ensure your code is formatted cleanly, variables are descriptively named, and outputs are verified in the console.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Input Validation Logic
docs.text:
Suppose an analytical function receives five parallel vectors containing sensor deployment data: 

buoy_ids     <- c("Buoy_01", "Buoy_02", "Buoy_03", "Buoy_04", "Buoy_05")
sensor_depth <- c(5.0, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0, 25.0)
salinity_psu <- c(34.2, 35.1, 33.8, 34.9, 35.5)
battery_pct  <- c(98.0, 85.5, 92.0, 78.0, 88.5)
is_active    <- c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)

Write logical checking expressions that test (without using if statements or loops):

  1. Whether all five vectors have the exact same length. (Tip: all vectors have the same length if each has the same length as buoy_ids.)
  2. Whether all values in sensor_depth, salinity_psu, and battery_pct are strictly positive (> 0).
  3. Whether battery_pct does not exceed 100.0 for any buoy.
  4. Combine these three tests into a single logical expression that evaluates to TRUE if and only if all validation criteria are met.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Vectorized Environmental Flux Calculation
docs.text:
A marine survey records water temperature and dissolved oxygen across 8 depth stations: 

temp_celsius    <- c(18.2, 17.5, 16.1, 14.8, 13.2, 12.0, 11.5, 10.8)
oxygen_mg_l     <- c(8.9,  8.5,  7.8,  7.2,  6.4,  5.8,  5.2,  4.9)

  1. The apparent metabolic oxygen consumption index (OCI) at each depth is estimated as: OCI = oxygen_mg_l x (1.5 + 0.08 x temp_celsius). Compute this for all stations and store the result in a vector named station_oci.
  2. Construct a logical vector hypoxic_risk identifying depths where temp_celsius < 15.0 and oxygen_mg_l < 6.0.
  3. Using hypoxic_risk as an index, extract the OCI values for the qualifying depths.
  4. Calculate the average OCI across these qualifying depths.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Sensor Outlier Masking
docs.text:
A coastal wave-monitoring buoy records wave height anomalies across 8 measurement cycles: 

wave_anomalies <- c(0.42, 1.85, NA, 0.78, 2.40, NA, 1.15, 0.95)
During stormy conditions, sensors can experience severe wave spray. Any reading from an active sensor that strictly exceeds a critical wave anomaly of 1.50 is considered corrupted and must be flagged. Sensors that were offline (NA) must remain flagged as FALSE (not corrupted).

  1. Write a single vectorized expression that creates a logical vector corrupted of length 8, where an element is TRUE if and only if the reading is non-missing and strictly greater than 1.50. Ensure corrupted contains only TRUE and FALSE values, with no NA entries.
  2. Using corrupted as an index, replace the corrupted readings in wave_anomalies with NA.
  3. Verify that uncorrupted valid measurements and previously missing readings remained in their proper states.

docs.title: Practical 2 - Introduction to Regular Expressions in R
Regular Expressions
docs.text:
Regular expressions are used to search for a specific pattern in a string. To understand them, we will take an example in which the actual names in our data file are incorrect, or inconsistent. Run the following line of code to import the a table into a data frame:

reptiles <- read.table(file = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MatthewHiggins2017/BIO773P/main/docs/data/reptiles.txt")

This data frame details the genus and species names of 16 endangered reptiles, along with the dates at which they were listed as endangered. You can load just the names into a separate variable by running the code

names_ids <- row.names(reptiles)

Have a close look at these names. Notice that each reptile has a unique identification number next to its name (don't look these numbers up - they don't mean anything)! Also, we can see that some names were recorded incorrectly - the genus names for the Liopholis group are in lowercase, while we all know that genus names should be capitalized! All in all, this data appears quite "messy" and needs cleaning up.

Regular expressions are ideal for fixing this. "Regex" are at the center of a suite of tools that allow us to search for, locate, and replace characters or words within a data set. The really powerful thing about regular expressions is that we can do a "fuzzy" search, meaning the pattern we are searching for has some flexibility built into it.

docs.title: Basic find and replace
docs.text:
First of all we will search through the vector names_ids to find a list of the elements that contain the word "liopholis". The function that allows us to do this is grep(), which has two main arguments; pattern and x. The pattern is the actual word, or part of a word, that we are looking for. The argument `x`` describes the variable that we are searching through. In our case we want to evaluate the following code:

# Search through names_ids for the word "liopholis", and output_positions
grep(pattern = "liopholis", x = names_ids)

The output of this code is a list of numbers. Each of these numbers describes the position of an element in the vector names_ids that matches the pattern - in this case the 12th and 13th elements. Make sure you fully understand where these numbers came from!

Sometimes it may be more useful to obtain the actual names within which the pattern was found, rather than a list of positions. We can do this by making use of the additional argument value = TRUE (see the help file for the grep() function for a complete list of possible arguments). The new code reads:

# Search through names_ids for the word "liopholis", and output_names
grep(pattern = "liopholis", x = names_ids, value = TRUE)

Now we find that the output contains the actual elements of the vector that match the pattern, rather than just a list of positions. These names correspond exactly with the positions found in the previous example.

Finally, we may want to find and replace the pattern. This can be done using the function gsub(). The function gsub() takes arguments pattern and x, just like the function grep(), but it also has an additional argument replacement. The argument replacement describes the new word, or words, that we want to insert in place of pattern. For example, in the reptiles the word "liopholis" is a genus name, and so should be capitalized. Thus, we want to replace the word "liopholis" with "Liopholis", as follows:

# Search through names_ids for the word "liopholis" and replace with the word "Liopholis".
names_ids_fixed <- gsub(pattern = "liopholis", replacement = "Liopholis", x = names_ids)

The output of this function is a new vector in which the desired replacement has been carried out. Notice that the code above stores this new vector in the variable names_ids_fixed.

Experiment with grep() and gsub() until you are confident at using them. Then answer the following questions:

docs.title: Q1. How could you use regular expressions to find the only element in the vector names_ids_fixed that contains a lowercase "q"? What is the position of this element in the vector?

Q2. You want to import the names_ids_fixed data into excel, but are having problems due to the spaces between the words (a common problem). How could you use gsub() to replace each space with an underscore _?
Using "fuzzy" searching
docs.text:
One of the most powerful features of regular expressions is the ability to perform "fuzzy" searching. Simply put, by using special characters we can introduce some flexibility into the pattern that we are searching for.

A slightly reduced list of special characters and their meanings is given below.

Special Character Meaning . Any character ? The preceding item is optional and will be matched at most once. * The preceding item will be matched zero or more times. + The preceding item will be matched one or more times.

Additional special characters can be found:

  • by Googling (e.g. "Regexp cheat sheet for R")
  • by typing: ?regex in R

These special characters can be used on their own, or in combination with one another. To help you out with understanding these symbols, here are a few examples:

  • The pattern .r means any character, followed by the letter "r" (e.g. "er", "or", "tr", "3r").
  • The pattern ...r means any character, followed by any character, followed by any character, followed by the letter "r" (e.g. "beer", "deer", "zekr").
  • The pattern l*at means zero or more copies of the letter "l", followed by the letters "at" (e.g. "at", "lat", "llllllllllat").
  • The pattern s.+s means the letter "s", followed by one or more copies of any character, followed by the letter "s" (e.g. "sas", "sts", "sauces", "serendipities", but NOT "ss").
  • The pattern .* .* means zero or more copies of any character, followed by a space, followed by zero or more copies of any character (any combination of two words, e.g. "test word").

Some of these examples might seem very confusing at first, but if you learn what each special character means on its own and then go through the pattern one at a time you should find that it makes sense.

As an example of how fuzzy searching can be useful, we will now use these special characters to remove the ID tags from the reptile names. Notice that the ID numbers are of different lengths, but they are always separated with a colon from the part that we are interested in. Therefore, we can remove these characters by searching for zero or more copies of any character, followed by a colon, and replacing this pattern with an empty string. The single line of code that achieves this is as follows:

names <- gsub(pattern = ".*:", replacement = "", x = names_ids_fixed)
Have a look inside the variable names. We have successfully isolated the genus and species names away from the pesky ID tags, even though the exact format of the tags may vary between different entries. Tricks like this can save us a great deal of time - especially when our data set is thousands of lines long. In fact, we have only skimmed the surface of what regular expressions can do - I encourage anyone who is interested to take a deeper look.

docs.title: Q3. What does the pattern "..x.." mean in a regular expression?
Q4. What does the pattern "e+" mean in a regular expression?
Q5a. How many reptile names in names contain a lowercase "o" or an uppercase "E"?
