docs.title: Q5b. How many reptile names in names contain "us" or "li"?
docs.text: Hint - As before, use a single grep command to identify the words with these patterns.

docs.title: Q6. Add three additional columns to the reptiles table:
docs.text:
• one containing only the identifier numbers (e.g. 1423 without the “ID”)
  • one column containing only the genus (e.g. "Bellatorias")
  • one containing only the species (excluding the genus name and the subspecies name, e.g. we want to read "tympanum")

Hint - try to decompose this task, the solution is not a “one-liner”. Make use of the functions you have just learnt and focus on extracting the numbers, genus, and species, rather than the “add new columns” bit.

docs.title: Data input from files
docs.text:
Open source data plays an increasingly important role recently, so it is vital to know how to input the data with various formats into your program. Choosing the right way of importing data will save you time and boost your efficiency when cleaning the data. To test your abilities, download longevity_genes/longevity.csv and TableS2.xls and try loading them into R.

longevity_genes_data  <- read.csv("input location/longevity.csv")
longevity_genes_data  <- read.csv(file.choose())                    # to choose the file
# try to figure out how to import Excel spreadsheets into R,
# which is an excessively discussed topic online.
# One way of doing it, is saving your Excel spreadsheet (TableS2.xls)
# as a tab delimited text file and loading it into R
read.delim("input location/file name.txt")

docs.title: Data output into various formats
docs.text:
Most of the time, as either a data recorder or a data analyst, knowing the best way to output data is important. Outputting data as a CSV file is recommended as it's compatible with both Excel and R.

# write a new subsetted data frame (create this using your previous skills) into a CSV file
write.csv(your_subsetted_data_frame, file = "output_location/file_name.csv")
# create three variables, a, b, and c of any class and save them into a .RData file (What is this? When could it be useful?)
save(a, b, c, file = "output_location/file_name.RData")

docs.title: Hacker Q7.  Download this text file and figure out how to “capture” the first letter of the genus, and transform it to make it uppercase. Do this in a generic manner (that would work on a table of thousands of species).
docs.text: Hint - look into the help page of “gsub”, especially the explanation for the “replacement” parameter, as well as the examples at the bottom of the help page.

docs.title: Practical 2 - Accessing and Manipulating Composite Data
Introduction
docs.text:
In Practical 1, we worked with atomic vectors, which store one-dimensional sequences of elements of the same data type. However, scientific datasets, laboratory surveys, and computational models require composite data structures capable of organizing multi-dimensional, multi-variable, or heterogeneous information:

  1. Matrices: Two-dimensional grids of values of a single atomic class (e.g., spatial grids, time-series profiles).
  2. Lists: Flexible, ordered collections where each element can be an entirely different type, length, or structure (e.g., grouping diverse survey metadata, sample vectors, and station parameters).
  3. Data Frames: The standard tabular format for statistical analysis in R, where rows represent individual observations and columns represent distinct variables of varying types.

In this practical, you will learn to construct, inspect, slice, modify, and aggregate each of these composite structures. Mastering these techniques will enable you to assemble structured data pipelines, validate multi-column datasets, and execute multi-condition filtering.

docs.title: Matrices: Two-Dimensional Grids
docs.text: A matrix is a two-dimensional rectangular array organized into rows and columns. Like an atomic vector, every cell in a matrix must contain the exact same data class (numeric, character, or logical).

docs.title: Creating Matrices
docs.text:
Matrices can be constructed using matrix() (please please copy and execute commands in boxes for later use of results; also make sure you understand each line of code; free free to play with the code to see what happens):

# Creating a matrix from a numeric sequence:
# By default, R populates matrices column-by-column:
mat1 <- matrix(data = 1:12, nrow = 4, ncol = 3)
mat1
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    1    5    9
# [2,]    2    6   10
# [3,]    3    7   11
# [4,]    4    8   12

# Fill row-by-row instead:
mat2 <- matrix(data = 1:12, nrow = 4, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
mat2
#      [,1] [,2] [,3]
# [1,]    1    2    3
# [2,]    4    5    6
# [3,]    7    8    9
# [4,]   10   11   12

We can also bind vectors of equal length together using rbind() (row bind) and cbind() (column bind): 

transect_a <- c(14.2, 15.1, 13.9)
transect_b <- c(16.0, 15.8, 16.4)

# Bind as rows (2 rows, 3 columns):
row_bound <- rbind(transect_a, transect_b)

# Bind as columns (3 rows, 2 columns):
col_bound <- cbind(transect_a, transect_b)

docs.title: Inspecting Matrix Dimensions and Naming
docs.text:
To check the dimensions of a matrix:

  • dim(m): Returns a vector c(nrow, ncol).
  • nrow(m): Total number of rows.
  • ncol(m): Total number of columns.

You can assign and query names for rows and columns: 

colnames(col_bound) <- c("Station_A", "Station_B")
rownames(col_bound) <- c("Depth_1m", "Depth_5m", "Depth_10m")
col_bound

docs.title: Matrix Subsetting and Slicing
docs.text:
Subsetting a matrix requires two indices inside square brackets: [row, column]. Remember the mnemonic: Row first, Column second (RC).

  • mat[r, c]: Element at row r, column c.
  • mat[r, ]: Entire row r (leaving the column blank extracts all columns).
  • mat[, c]: Entire column c (leaving the row blank extracts all rows).
  • mat[c(1, 3), c(2, 3)]: Sub-grid spanning rows 1 & 3 and columns 2 & 3.
# Using mat1 from above:
mat1[2, 3]        # 10
mat1[1:2, ]       # First two rows across all columns
mat1[, 2]         # Entire second column: 5 6 7 8

Note on Dimension Dropping: When you extract a single row or single column (e.g., mat1[, 2]), R automatically drops the matrix dimensions and returns a simple 1D vector. If you wish to preserve the 2D matrix structure, supply drop = FALSE: 

mat1[, 2, drop = FALSE]  # Returns a 4x1 matrix

docs.title: Matrix Arithmetic and Margins
docs.text:
Mathematical operations on matrices occur element-by-element: 

mat1 * 5
mat1 + mat2

To summarize rows or columns efficiently, use R's built-in margin functions:

  • rowSums(m), colSums(m): Sum totals across rows or columns.
  • rowMeans(m), colMeans(m): Arithmetic averages across rows or columns.
colMeans(mat1)  # 2.5 6.5 10.5

docs.title: Q1. Consider the matrix:
docs.text:
sample_grid <- matrix(data = seq(10, 180, by = 10), nrow = 6, ncol = 3)
Without executing the code first:

  1. How many total elements are in sample_grid?
  2. What value is located at sample_grid[4, 2]?
  3. Write an expression to replace all values in sample_grid strictly greater than 100 with 100.

docs.title: Lists: Heterogeneous and Hierarchical Data
docs.text:
Atomic vectors and matrices are restricted to holding elements of one atomic class. A list, however, is a generic vector that can contain elements of any class, length, or structure—including vectors of different lengths, matrices, data frames, or other lists.

Lists are widely used in R to bundle related parameters, package complex experimental outputs, or return grouped records.

docs.title: Creating Lists
docs.text:
Lists are constructed using list(). Giving each element a descriptive name makes downstream retrieval clear and robust:

expedition_record <- list(
  vessel_name     = "R/V Discovery",
  cruise_id       = 104L,
  sensor_readings = c(12.4, 13.1, 12.8, 14.0),
  gps_active      = TRUE,
  salinity_psu    = c(34.1, 34.2, 34.0)
)

In the Environment tab of RStudio, click the blue expand arrow next to expedition_record to inspect its hierarchical structure.

docs.title: Accessing List Elements: [ vs [[ vs $
docs.text:
Understanding the distinction between single brackets [ and double brackets [[ is important when working with lists:

  • Single Brackets [ ] (Sub-listing): Extracts a slice of the list. It always returns a list, even if you request only a single element: 

    sub <- expedition_record["vessel_name"]
class(sub)  # "list"
    Analogy: Think of a list as a train with cargo wagons. expedition_record[1] uncouples the 1st wagon and hands you a shorter train consisting of that single wagon.

  • Double Brackets [[ ]] (Element Extraction): Extracts the actual object stored inside the designated position or name: 

    name_val <- expedition_record[["vessel_name"]]
class(name_val)  # "character"
    Analogy: expedition_record[[1]] opens up the 1st wagon, unloads the cargo inside, and hands you the cargo directly.

  • Dollar Sign $ (Named Extraction): Convenient shorthand for [[ "name" ]]: 

    expedition_record$sensor_readings  # Returns numeric vector: 12.4 13.1 12.8 14.0


# You can immediately apply vector operations to extracted elements:
mean(expedition_record$sensor_readings)  # 13.075

docs.title: Accessing the Names of List Elements
docs.text:
You can see and modify the names of list elements using the names() command:

# List the names of all elements:
record_names <- names(expedition_record)
record_names

# Modify a name:
names(expedition_record)[which(record_names == "sensor_readings")] <-
    "sensor_readings_mA"

docs.title: Modifying and Adding List Elements
docs.text:
You can update existing elements, add new entries, or delete elements by assignment:

# Modify existing element:
expedition_record$gps_active <- FALSE

# Add a new element:
expedition_record$chief_scientist <- "Dr. Vance"

# Remove an element by assigning NULL:
expedition_record$cruise_id <- NULL

See how expedition_record changed in the Environment tab.

docs.title: Nested Lists
docs.text:
Because list elements can be any object, you can nest lists within lists. This hierarchical structure is standard for multi-site monitoring campaigns or complex parameter configurations:

station_reports <- list(
  Station_Alpha = list(temp = 14.2, turbidity = 2.1, certified = TRUE,  depth = 45.0),
  Station_Beta  = list(temp = 11.5, turbidity = 5.8, certified = FALSE, depth = 85.0),
  Station_Gamma = list(temp = 16.8, turbidity = 1.4, certified = TRUE,  depth = 32.5)
)

# Extract information for a specific station:
station_reports[["Station_Alpha"]]$temp        # 14.2
station_reports$Station_Gamma$certified        # TRUE

docs.title: Q2. Given station_reports above:
docs.text:
1. Write an expression to retrieve the turbidity at Station_Beta.
  2. Add a new station named "Station_Delta" to station_reports containing temperature 13.4, turbidity 3.0, certified status TRUE, and depth 60.0.
  3. Assuming that value of station_name is a character expression (e.g., station_name <- "Station_Gamma"), giving the name of a station, extract the report of the station with that name.

docs.title: Data Frames: Tabular Scientific Datasets
docs.text:
A data frame is a two-dimensional table designed specifically for statistical data analysis. Formally, a data frame is a named list of vectors of identical length, where:

  • Each column represents a variable (and must be of a single atomic class).
  • Each row represents an observation (and can span multiple classes across columns).

Unlike a matrix (which forces all cells into one atomic type), a data frame holds numeric, character, and logical columns side by side.

docs.title: Creating Data Frames
docs.text:
Construct data frames using data.frame():

estuary_df <- data.frame(
  station_id    = 101:106,
  salinity_psu  = c(28.4, 32.1, 29.5, 34.8, 31.0, 33.2),
  sampling_depth = c(2.5,  5.0,  3.0, 12.0,  8.5,  4.0),
  sediment_type  = c("Sand", "Mud", "Sand", "Gravel", "Mud", "Sand"),
  is_marine      = c(FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

estuary_df

Inspect the structure and dimensions of your data frame: 

dim(estuary_df)      # 6 rows, 5 columns
nrow(estuary_df)     # 6
ncol(estuary_df)     # 5
names(estuary_df)    # Column names
str(estuary_df)      # Structure overview
head(estuary_df, 3)  # First 3 rows

docs.title: Accessing Columns and Cells
docs.text:
Columns can be extracted as vectors using $, [[ ]], or [, "column_name"]:

# Extract a column as an atomic vector:
estuary_df$salinity_psu
estuary_df[["salinity_psu"]]
estuary_df[, "salinity_psu"]

# Extract a specific cell: row 2, column 'salinity_psu':
estuary_df[2, "salinity_psu"]  # 32.1

docs.title: Adding and Computing New Columns
docs.text:
You can add new variables directly or compute them from existing columns using vectorized expressions:

# Compute an estimated hydraulic pressure index:
# pressure = sampling_depth * (1.0 + 0.02 * salinity_psu)

estuary_df$pressure_idx <- estuary_df$sampling_depth * (1.0 + 0.02 * estuary_df$salinity_psu)

estuary_df

docs.title: Subsetting and Filtering Data Frames
docs.text: Data analysis routinely requires filtering data frames to isolate rows meeting environmental or experimental criteria.

docs.title: 1. Filtering with Row Logical Indexing
docs.text:
The standard and most robust method to filter a data frame is passing a logical condition into the row index position: df[condition, ].

# Find stations where salinity is strictly greater than 30.0:
saline_stations <- estuary_df[estuary_df$salinity_psu > 30.0, ]
saline_stations

# Combine multiple conditions:
# Salinity > 30.0 AND sampling depth >= 5.0:
deep_saline_df <- estuary_df[estuary_df$salinity_psu > 30.0 & estuary_df$sampling_depth >= 5.0, ]
deep_saline_df

Crucial Syntax Reminder: Do not forget the comma inside the brackets! * estuary_df[condition, ] filters rows and keeps all columns. * estuary_df[condition] would attempt to subset columns by name or index and cause errors.

docs.title: 2. Filtering with subset()
docs.text:
R also provides the helper function subset(), which evaluates column names directly:

deep_saline_sub <- subset(estuary_df, salinity_psu > 30.0 & sampling_depth >= 5.0)

While subset() is convenient for quick interactive exploration, bracket indexing df[condition, ] is preferred inside scripted functions and packages due to unambiguous variable evaluation rules.

docs.title: Aggregation and Boundary Cases
docs.text:
Consider a situation where, once a data frame is filtered, summary statistics are calculated across specific columns, e.g.:

# Calculate the mean pressure index of the deep saline stations:
mean_pressure <- mean(deep_saline_df$pressure_idx)
mean_pressure

docs.title: Boundary Case: Zero Qualifying Rows
docs.text:
In computational pipelines and simulations, it is common that no observations satisfy the filtering criterion. Your code must handle empty subsets predictably:

# Filter for extreme criteria that do not occur in our data:
extreme_df <- estuary_df[estuary_df$salinity_psu > 45.0 & estuary_df$sampling_depth > 50.0, ]

nrow(extreme_df)  # Returns 0

If you calculate the mean of an empty numeric vector: 

mean(extreme_df$pressure_idx)  # Returns NaN (Not a Number)

To handle such situations in complicated scripts, you can check whether nrow(df) > 0:

# Checking if rows exist before computing summary:
has_rows <- nrow(extreme_df) > 0
has_rows  # FALSE

docs.title: Missing Data in Data Frames
docs.text:
Tabular datasets frequently contain missing values (NA). 

field_records <- data.frame(
  plot_id     = 1:4,
  temperature = c(15.2, NA, 18.1, 14.7),
  dissolved_o2 = c(7.8, 8.1, NA, 6.9)
)
  • is.na(field_records): Returns a logical matrix indicating missing cells across the table.
  • complete.cases(field_records): Returns a logical vector of length nrow, which is TRUE only for rows that have no missing values in any column.
  • na.omit(field_records): Strips out all rows containing any NA.
complete.cases(field_records)  # TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE

clean_records <- field_records[complete.cases(field_records), ]
clean_records
#   plot_id temperature dissolved_o2
# 1       1        15.2          7.8
# 4       4        14.7          6.9

docs.title: Practical 3 - Introduction to functions and loops in R
docs.text: Building on your existing skills, we will now move on to consider advanced ways of controlling program flow. Specifically, we will explore functions and loops, two important features of R that are also present in most other programming languages. We will also be doing a few exercises with DNA/RNA strings. As always, you will want to refer frequently to the R help files (through ?) and your own notes when exploring these new concepts.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Functions are pieces of code that take input information (in the form of "arguments"), do something with it, and give back an output. They allow you to run an analysis multiple times without having to rewrite it from scratch every time you need to run it. A function looks like this:

function_name <- function(input) {

  ### the "body" of the function

  # code that performs some calculation on the input
  # possibly other lines of code that perform calculations

  # returning an output vector:
  return(output)
}

You can choose whatever name you want instead of function_name (try a meaningful name). After the <-, the word function within brackets lets R know that you are writing a new function. Here, input is the name of the only argument that the calculations in the body of the function are based on (your function can have multiple arguments). Between the curly brackets {} is the main code of your function, where the calculation(s) happen. Almost everything that occurs between the curly brackets stays within the curly brackets. The only thing that comes outside the curly brackets is what you put into the return() on the last line. If you have no return(), your function may compute something but nobody will ever know about it! Note that the return command can only handle a single argument.

To take a self-explanatory example:

x <- c(2, 3, 4, 5)
mean(x)

You just used the mean function, one of many functions that our predecessors built into R. The point of this function is that you can calculate the mean of any vector without explicitly writing the formula for the mean each time. The interesting thing about R is that it is possible to create your own functions. This is how R functions work:

## Define function named 'my_own_mean'

my_own_mean <- function(numbers) {
  ## Calculate mean
  # Sum all numbers in the vector
  sum_of_values <- sum(numbers)

  # Obtain the number of values in the vector
  number_of_values <- length(numbers)

  # Get the mean
  mean_value <- sum_of_values/number_of_values

  ## Output the mean
  return(mean_value)
}

## Now run the function with some data:
my_own_mean(numbers = c(10, 20, 30, 40))

my_own_mean(numbers = seq(from = 1, to = 50))

We created a function that computes the sum and number of all values in a given vector (numbers) and then divides them to obtain the mean. We split the calculation in three steps, just to show that you can have many lines of code in the body of a function. The only input this function receives is a vector of numbers (numbers) and all the calculations are based on this. In the end we return the result of the third calculation (mean_value). Does number_of_values exist in the normal R console? No! Because this variable was only created within the curly brackets. Remember? What happens between the curly brackets stays in the curly brackets.

Nothing much happens after loading the function my_own_mean into R (you always have to evaluate the entire code of the function from function_name to the closing curly brackets } if you made changes to the code). The magic happens when you call the function. We did this by typing my_own_mean(numbers = 1:50) (of course you can use other vectors instead as well). The vector with numbers from 1 to 50 will be used as numbers in the function.

Now take a look at the following lines of code. This code is designed to take a number in seconds and convert it into hours, minutes, and remaining seconds (floor() is R's built-in function for rounding down to the closest whole number):

# Input raw number of seconds
number_of_seconds <- 19955

# Convert number_of_seconds into hours, minutes, and seconds
hours   <- floor(number_of_seconds / (60 * 60))
minutes <- floor((number_of_seconds - hours * (60 * 60)) / 60)
seconds <- number_of_seconds - ((hours * 60) + minutes) * 60

# Create a single vector containing all three quantities
outputs <- c(hours, minutes, seconds)

# Output the solution to the console
outputs

docs.title: Q1. Modify the code above to make it into a function called time_converter. This function should take a single number as an argument (the number of seconds we want to convert). This function should also include the three lines of code that convert number_of_seconds into hours, minutes, and seconds, the line of code that merges these three variables into one vector, and a line returning this vector as the output of the function. Once you created the function and loaded it into R, use relevant examples for testing (0, 3600, another). Remember to indent any code inside the curly brackets.

Q2. Write your own function for converting distances between different units. Your function should take the distance in kilometres as input and return the distance in miles as output (1 kilometre is 0.6213712 miles). Note: floor won't be needed in the calculations here. Remember to clearly comment/annotate your code and make appropriate use of whitespace including indentation and newlines.
More complex functions
docs.text:
Functions can be very useful when you have to do the same calculation many times. We will now consider a hypothetical experiment in which we are measuring the flight speed of bees through flight tunnels.

We would like to measure the flight speed of the bees in meters per second. Annoyingly, the timer we used gave readings with the format hours:minutes:seconds, rather than just the total number of seconds.

Fortunately, functions in R can take more than one argument:

my_function <- function(input1, input2, ...) {
    # code including input1, input2, ...
    return(something)
}

docs.title: Q3. Make a function that takes hours, minutes and seconds as inputs, and outputs the total number of seconds. Make sure it has three arguments and a descriptive name. Test the function with a range of times for which you know the answer.
docs.text:
In our experiment, most bees flew through the test tunnel in under an hour. It is time consuming to include the argument hours = 0 every time that we call the function.

A neat thing about functions is that we can set default values for any argument, using the syntax:

my_function <- function(input1, ..., input15 = default) {
  # code including input1, input2, ..., input15
  return(something)
}

The default argument(s) is generally placed at the end of the argument list.

docs.title: Q4. Make the hours and minutes arguments be defined as 0 by default in your function. Run the function without supplying these two arguments, then run it again with using a range of hours and minutes.
docs.text:
Finally, we would like to create a function to measure the flight speed of the bees in meters per second. This function should:

  • Take the tunnel length (in meters), hours, minutes and seconds as arguments
  • Use your previous function to convert hours, minutes and seconds to seconds
  • Calculate the speed of the bees in meters per second
  • Return the speed of the bees

docs.title: Q5A. Create this function. Test it with a control (values for which you know the answer).
Q5B. Use the function to measure the speed of the bees with the following measurements:
docs.text: Distance (m) Time (hours:minutes:seconds) 1 00:00:08 10 00:00:40 300 00:05:00 800 01:06:40

docs.title: Q5C. Can you think of parameter values that would make your function not work properly? What happens if you try running the function with these values?
Functions with other types of input
docs.text: Note that functions do not have to take single numbers as input. They can take vectors, matrices, data frames, or any other type of object, and they can also take character and logical data as well as numerical. For example, the mean function we used earlier took the vector x <- c(2, 3, 4, 5) as input, which is a single vector with four numbers.

docs.title: Q6. Write a function that takes a vector of words as input and outputs the number of characters in the longest word. Hint: you are going to need to find out how R counts the number of characters in words and how it finds the maximum value in a vector - use an internet search engine!
Loops
docs.text:
Imagine that you need to run the function time_converter on different numbers. You could type time_converter many different times, each time with a different number. But now imagine you had to type that thousands of times. Not fun.

Fortunately, computers were built to perform same tasks over and over again many times. They do this using a construct called a loop. Although there are several types of loops, we are going to learn about the 'for loop'. It works this way:

## For loop example
for (seconds in c(1000, 2000, 3000)) {
  time_in_hours <- time_converter(number_of_seconds = seconds)
  print(time_in_hours)
}

The variable seconds only exists within the loop. The loop will run 3 times. The first time, seconds will take the first value from the vector (1000, 2000, 3000), i.e., 1000. R will run through the loop, computing time_in_hours and printing it. When R starts running through the loop the second time, seconds will have the value 2000, and the previously calculated time_in_hours will have been forgotten. R will run through the loop, computing time_in_hours and printing it. The third time, same thing again, but seconds will start with the value 3000.

docs.title: Slightly more complex loops
docs.text:
There are some interesting ways in which we can stretch our understanding of loops. First of all, it is important to recognise that the values that we are iterating over can be anything that goes in a vector. The vector can be defined outside the loop definition line:

## Character based loop values
greetings <- c("Hey", "Hi", "Hello", "Aloha", "Howdy",
               "Yooooo!", "Wassup", "What's shakin?",
               "yello!", "Greetings",  "Dude, wake up!")
for (word in greetings) {
  print(paste(word, " - said the giggling frog", sep = " "))
}

## Sequential loop values
my_favourite_numbers <- c(42, 3.14, 7, 69, 6.626e-34, 1024, 4, 2.718281828, 666, 1.61803398, 99)

# set the cumulative sum at zero before the loop starts
cumulative_sum <- 0

for (value in my_favourite_numbers) {
  # print the sentence
  print(paste(value, "is my favourite number", sep = " "))

  # add favourite numbers, sequentially
  cumulative_sum <- cumulative_sum + value

  # print the cumulative sum
  print(paste("The sum of my favourite numbers is:", cumulative_sum, sep = " "))
}

## Looping through the positions of each element of the vector (the index, or position)
foods <- c("tempeh", "beyond", "beans", "tofu")
for (position in seq_len(length(foods))) {
  current_food <- foods[position]
  message("At position ", position, " we have ", current_food)
}

docs.title: Storing loop results
docs.text:
You will often want to do more than just print the loop results. For example, you may want to keep them in a separate variable. Check the following example. What does phrases look like after the 4th iteration?

## Vector to loop through
practical_attributes <- c("great", "deeply distressing", "very long", "amazeballs!", "informative")

## Empty vector to store the loop results in
phrases <- c()

for (practical_attribute in practical_attributes) {
 phrase <- paste("This practical is", practical_attribute)
 # Add the loop result to end of the vector of results
 phrases <- append(phrases, phrase)
}

A different way of approaching a for loop is to loop through the positions of a vector, rather than the vector itself. In the following code, we also create a vector for the result with the same length as the vector that we are looping through. We then use the position to 'populate' it:

## Vector to loop through
practical_attributes <- c("great", "deeply distressing", "very long", "amazeballs!", "informative")

## Vector with empty elements (as long as practical_attributes)
phrases <- rep("", times = length(practical_attributes))

## Loop through the position rather than the vector
for (position in 1:length(practical_attributes)) {

  ## Create phrase, getting attribute from practical_attributes[i]
  phrase <- paste("This practical is", practical_attributes[position])

  ## Add phrase to the right position of the results vector
  phrases[position] <- phrase
}

It is important to understand these two approaches with loops: looping through items vs. looping through positions. In some contexts it is easier to use the first approach; in other contexts the second is easier. Once you are comfortable with loops, have a go at the following tasks:

docs.title: Pen and paper Q7. Consider the following table, which lists the genus and species name for a number of ant species present in Great Britain. The loop counts the number of entries where the genus name begins with given letters. Describe in your own words what the loop is doing at each iteration.

for (letter in letters){
 begins_with <- paste("^", letter, sep = "")
 matches <- grep(pattern = begins_with, x = ant_table$genus)

}

Write a loop that iterates over the colours red, green, blue, yellow, orange, purple, pink and prints out the position (i.e. the position of the colour in the vector) and the colour itself. Using loops
docs.text: For the following exercice, imagine that instead of buying a coffee, you deposit the £2.50 you would have spent into a savings account. The account has an annual interest rate of 5%, which is deposited into the account. You do not take any money out of the account for 20 years.

Q10. Create a plot showing the amount of money in the account for each year. Hint: If you have not already done so, you will need to create a vector to store the account balance for each year. You can use the base R function plot(), or, if you are feeling adventurous, install the "ggplot2" package and use that! See https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/articles/ggplot2.html for more information.
docs.text: In the following exercise, we will simulate the size of a population given a reproduction rate that changes every year.

docs.title: Q11. Write a loop that calculates the population size depending on the reproduction rate over a period of 20 years. Store the population value for each iteration of the loop in a separate vector.

• Use a starting population size of 1000.
  • Every year,
  • obtain a random reproduction rate (e.g., reproduction_rate <- rnorm(n = 1, mean = 1, sd = 0.4).
  • Update the population size value accordingly.

docs.title: Nested Loops
docs.text:
Another important way of extending loops is to consider nested loops - in other words, loops within other loops! Have a look at the following code:

coffee <- c("latte", "cappuccino", "flat white", "cortado")
cafes   <- c("Infusion", "Ground", "Sugar Cube", "Foxcroft & Ginger", "Sweet")

for (drink in coffees) {
  print(paste("I'd like a", drink, "... Where can I go?"))
  for (the_place in cafes) {
    print(paste("You can go to", the_place, "to have a", drink))
  }
}

Here we have one loop (with position the_place) nested within another loop (with position drink). We have also defined the values that the_place and drink can take. With a pen and paper, determine what is the 1st line printed, and then what is the 10th line printed? Evaluate this code and try to make sense of the output. Fiddle around with the different elements of this code until you are comfortable with nested loops. Warning - loops require your computer to perform many operations, and as such it is quite easy to crash R using loops. A simple block of code evaluated 100,000 times amounts to quite a big job. If you want to force R to exit a loop part way through, simply press 'Esc' (or control-C). Nested loops are particularly hazardous!

docs.title: Q12-A. Create a nested loop. The outer loop should iterate over the words "Angry", "Lazy", and "Happy". The inner loop should iterate over the words "birds", "dogs", and "horses". The code inside the inner loop should print out a vector containing the values of both loops (for example "Angry" and "birds" in the first instance).

Q12-B. Look again at the code you wrote in Q12-A. Did you sufficiently indent your code (like in the example of a nested loop above), so that it is easy to see which lines of code are executed at which point of the different loops? If not, DO IT NOW! And continue doing it for the next questions as well.
Q13. Write a third-degree nested loop (i.e. a loop within a loop within a loop). Be careful not to loop over too many values or you will crash R!
docs.text: (if you're short of ideas, you could for example add practical_attributes qualifiers to Q12...)

docs.title: Using loops to reformat a data set
docs.text:
Loops are particularly useful to reformat data sets. By looping through all of the fields of a particular data set and at each iteration saving the relevant entry into a new data structure, it is possible to convert from one data format into another.

The data set that we will use in this example is typical of the sort of data that you might be faced with in the future. Load the data by running the following line of code:

helianthus_data <- as.matrix(read.table("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MatthewHiggins2017/BIO773P/main/docs/data/HelianthusData_num.txt",
                                         header = TRUE))

Each row in this data set represents a different strain of Helianthus annuus (sunflowers), grown under controlled conditions. The first column tells us the Strain (these are numbered from 1 to 5). The remaining columns describe the number of plants found in the study area at six different points in time. For example, looking at the first row, we can see that strain 1 started out with 12 plants in the first time point and ended up with 57 plants in the last time point.

We want to get this data into a new format - sometimes called long format - in which we have a matrix of three columns; the first column describes the strain, the second column describes the time point, and the third column describes the number of plants observed. It turns out that researchers often need to do this! For example, plotting using ggplot (and many analysis packages) requires long format. The first few lines of this new data structure should look like this:

strain time count 1 0 12 1 1 33 1 2 71 1 3 61 1 4 73 1 5 57 2 0 10 2 1 27 ... ... ...

We can make the transition from the wide format of helianthus_data to the long format described above using a nested loop. But first, let us create an empty matrix, which we will eventually fill with our new values.

docs.title: Q14-A. Create an empty matrix, called long_data. This matrix must have 3 columns and 30 rows (the number 30 comes from the fact that we have five strains at six time points each). Name the columns c("strain", "time", "count").
docs.text:
With this empty matrix created, we can move on to the next part of the problem - populating it with values. We want to look at each of the elements of helianthus_data one after the other, using a nested loop. The basic structure of this nested loop is as follows:

# Loop through all rows of helianthus_data
nrow(helianthus_data)
for (my_rows in 1:5) {
  # Loop through all columns of helianthus_data except the first
  for (my_col in 2:7) {

    # This is where the main code goes (populating long_data with values).

  }
}

Here we are using loops to go through each of the rows of the matrix helianthus_data, and for each row we are going through columns 2 to 7 (as these are the columns that contain relevant data). At any point in the two loops, the value that we are focusing on is given by helianthus_data[my_rows, my_col].

Hopefully you can already see that these are the exact values that we want to drop into the third column of our matrix long_data. However, we are presented with a problem - how do we drop these values one after the other into the right place in the matrix long_data? We cannot use the index my_rows to help us, as this only goes through values 1 to 5. Similarly, we cannot use the index my_col, as this only goes through values 2 to 7. What we really need is a new index that goes all the way from 1 to 30, irrespectively of the row or column that we are focusing on.

docs.title: Q14-B. Change the for loop above to include a variable my_position. This variable should be defined as being 0 before the loop starts. At every iteration of the inner loop, you should add 1 to it. What are the values of my_rows and my_col when my_position is 3? Add a line to check the positions each time through.
docs.text:
It should look something like this:

# my_position defined as 0 before the loop starts
my_position <- 0

# Loop through all rows
for (my_row in 1:5) {
  # Loop through all columns except the first
  for (my_col in 2:7) {

    ## Change my_position here:
    # make my_position equal to my_position plus one

    # Print all the indices here to check that you are doing the right thing
  }
}

Now that we have three indices - one going through the rows of helianthus_data, one going through the columns of helianthus_data, and one simply going from 1 to 30 - we have all the ingredients we need to populate the matrix long_data. The code we need at each iteration of the loop is the following:

# Get Count
long_data[my_position, 3] <- helianthus_data[my_row, my_col]

This is fairly straightforward. We also want to drop the time point in the second column of long_data. Although we do not have a vector describing each of the time points, in fact the timings are very simply given by 'my_col minus two'. For example, if we are looking at the fourth column then we are looking at the second time point. Therefore, we need the following line of code to extract the timings:

# Get Time
long_data[my_position, 2] <- my_col - 2

Finally, we want to drop the strain type into the first column of long_data. The strain type is given by the first element in every row, meaning it is given by helianthus_data[my_rows, 1]. Therefore, we need the following line of code to extract the strain types:

# Get Strain
long_data[my_position, 1] <- helianthus_data[my_rows, 1]

docs.title: Q14-C. Bring all of this together to finish the for loop, and run it!
docs.text:
To check what you've done, you can print the start and end of long_data:

head(long_data)
tail(long_data)

Hacker section: Working with DNA data
Bonus Q15-A. Write a function that converts a short DNA sequence of 15 bases (e.g. "ACCTGTCATCATCCC") to RNA and splits the string into codon triplets. You will need to:
docs.text:
• load the data into R: dna_string <- scan("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MatthewHiggins2017/BIO773P/main/docs/data/sequence.txt", what = character())
  • replace T with U (thymine with uracil to convert DNA to RNA)
  • use substring() to split the sequence into triplets and seq() within substring()
  • return the RNA triplets string

Note substring() takes a 'first' and 'last' argument. The 'first' would be a sequence indicating where the beginnings of your triplets are. The 'last' argument would be a sequence indicating where the ends of your triplets are. In seq() you will also indicate you want triplets.

As an example:

dna_string <- c("AAATTT")
substring(dna_string, seq(from = 1, to = 4, by = 3), seq(from = 3, to = 6, by = 3))

docs.title: Bonus Q15-B. Once you have created the function, see if you can modify it to work for a sequence with any number of characters. Tip: you can use nchar() to create a variable such as num_characters.
Bonus Q16. Write a function to obtain the reverse-complement of a DNA sequence.
docs.text:
You can use this sequence (copy and paste it into R): "ATTACGACGCGATTCCCGGTTAATCGAATTCCCA". As an example, the reverse-complement of ATGC is GCAT.

The tricky part here is reversing a single string of characters. Search around for strsplit. You will need to:

  • replace bases with their complement (you can use gsub, judiciously replacing uppercase characters with lowercase characters (or vice-versa)).
  • split the string of DNA bases into separate characters with strsplit. Unfortunately, strsplit confusingly returns a list, so you will need to use unlist() to obtain a string again.
  • reverse the sequence.
  • remove the spaces to get your single string of DNA bases (look into the help files for the paste() function).
  • return the reverse-complement sequence.

docs.title: Mastermind Q17. Translate your triplet string from Q15 into amino acids.
docs.text: Note: depending on your method, you may not need to convert it to RNA first. You can use a codon-to-amino-acid table and code the translation yourself. Your solution could include a function calling a function. Alternatively, you could search around and load a specific package for the manipulation of biological sequences.

docs.title: Bringing it all together
docs.text:
Well done for making it this far! Now try to bring all of your knowledge together. Have another look over your previous notes and make sure these ideas are still fresh in your mind. Have a go at writing your own scripts, preferably combining a number of different concepts (for example, you could try making a function that acts on a matrix and then using this function within a loop). Another good idea would be to come up with a problem that you want to solve (either for fun or for other coursework) and then write a function that solves it.

Many of the ideas presented in this and the last session are designed to challenge you. Do not expect to understand them from a single read through the material. Rather, you will have to play around with many different examples and applications before the penny drops completely. On the plus side, structures such as loops and functions are common to almost all programming languages, and so once you understand these concepts the world of programming is your oyster!

docs.title: Practical 3 - Functions, Flow Control, and Defensive Programming
Introduction
docs.text:
In Practicals 1 and 2, you learned how to manipulate atomic vectors and composite structures (matrices, lists, and data frames) using vectorized expressions. In this practical, we shift from executing one-off commands to constructing reusable code.

Modern scientific workflows require code that is modular, transparent, and robust against unexpected inputs. You will learn to:

  1. Encapsulate logic into custom functions with formal arguments, default parameters, and controlled return values.
  2. Implement defensive programming by validating input types, checking dimensions, and halting execution with informative error messages (stop()).
  3. Control execution flow using scalar conditional branching (if / else if / else).
  4. Automate repetitive computations using pre-allocated loops (for / while), including iteration skips (next) and loop termination (break).
  5. Combine function definitions to for more difficult tasks.

We will focus on breaking down multi-step scientific problems into clear, verifiable programmatic statements.

docs.title: The Anatomy of an R Function
docs.text:
A function is an encapsulated, named block of code that accepts inputs (arguments), executes a set of instructions, and returns an output object.

Functions provide four decisive advantages in scientific programming:

  • Elimination of Duplication: You write and debug a calculation once, rather than copying and pasting lines across your script.
  • Isolation (Scope): Variables created inside a function exist only during its execution. They do not pollute or overwrite variables in your global workspace.
  • Testability: You can systematically test a function against edge cases to ensure its computational correctness.
  • Encapsulation: Once you (or somebody else) has written a working R function, you (or others) only need to understand intuitively what it does rather than considering the details of how it is (best) done.

docs.title: Basic Syntax and Return Values
docs.text:
Functions are created using the function keyword and assigned to a variable name using <-:

# Define a function to calculate acoustic sound velocity in seawater (Mackenzie, 1981):
calc_sound_speed <- function(temp_c, salinity_psu, depth_m) {
  speed <- 1448.96 + 4.591 * temp_c - 0.05304 * (temp_c^2) + 
           1.340 * (salinity_psu - 35.0) + 0.0163 * depth_m
  return(speed)
}

To execute (call) the function, pass the arguments by position or by name:

# By position:
calc_sound_speed(12.5, 34.2, 250.0)

# By name (preferred for clarity and order independence):
calc_sound_speed(depth_m = 250.0, temp_c = 12.5, salinity_psu = 34.2)

Rules of Return:

  1. In R, return(value) explicitly terminates the function and passes value back to the caller.
  2. If return() is omitted, R automatically returns the last evaluated expression in the function body. However, in scientific programming, writing explicit return() statements makes your exit points unambiguous.
  3. A function can return only one single object. If you need to return multiple pieces of information (e.g., a numeric summary, a filtered data frame, and a status flag), package them into a named list.

docs.title: Default Arguments
docs.text:
You can provide fallback default values for arguments in the function header:

calc_hydrostatic_pressure <- function(depth_m, gravity = 9.80665, water_density = 1025.0) {
  # pressure in kiloPascals (kPa)
  pressure_kpa <- (water_density * gravity * depth_m) / 1000.0
  return(pressure_kpa)
}

# Uses defaults for gravity and water density:
calc_hydrostatic_pressure(depth_m = 100.0)

# Overrides water density for freshwater lake:
calc_hydrostatic_pressure(depth_m = 100.0, water_density = 1000.0)

docs.title: Variable Scoping: Local vs Global
docs.text:
Consider this scenario:

calibration_offset <- 1.5

adjust_reading <- function(reading) {
  adjusted <- reading + calibration_offset
  return(adjusted)
}

adjust_reading(10.0)  # Returns 11.5

The function was able to find calibration_offset in the global environment even though it was not passed as an argument. This is dangerous practice. If calibration_offset is renamed, modified, or cleared from memory later in your session, your function will break or return incorrect numbers without warning.

Golden Rule of Modularity: A function should be a self-contained "black box". It should rely only on arguments explicitly passed into it and variables defined locally within its body.

docs.title: Q1. Consider the function:
docs.text:
estimate_heat_content <- function(temp_c, water_mass_kg, specific_heat = 4184) {
  joules <- water_mass_kg * specific_heat * temp_c
  return(joules)
}
  1. What value is returned by estimate_heat_content(20.0, 50.0)?
  2. If you evaluate joules in your console after running this function, what happens? Why?

docs.title: Defensive Programming and Input Validation
docs.text:
When writing scripts for your own use, you might know what inputs are expected. However, in production pipelines, shared repositories, and testing during assessments, functions frequently receive incorrect, incomplete, or corrupted inputs.

Defensive programming means designing your function to inspect its arguments before performing calculations, verifying that all preconditions hold, and immediately halting with an informative error message if an inconsistency is detected.

docs.title: Halting Execution with stop()
docs.text:
The stop() function interrupts execution immediately, aborts any ongoing calculations, and prints an error message to the console:

validate_temperature <- function(temp_c) {
  if (temp_c < -273.15) {
    stop("Input temperature cannot be below absolute zero (-273.15 C).")
  }
  return(temp_c + 273.15)
}

validate_temperature(-300.0)
# Error in validate_temperature(-300): Input temperature cannot be below absolute zero (-273.15 C).

docs.title: Essential Validation Checks
docs.text:
Every robust scientific function should validate its inputs against four structural criteria:

  1. Dimensionality / Length: Is the input a single scalar, or a vector of expected length? 
    if (length(x) != 1) {
  stop("Argument 'x' must be a scalar (vector of length 1).")
}
  2. Data Type / Class: Does the input conform to the required atomic class? 
    if (!is.numeric(x)) {
  stop("Argument 'x' must be numeric.")
}
  3. Missingness: Does the input contain forbidden NA or NaN values? 
    if (is.na(x)) {
  stop("Argument 'x' cannot be NA.")
}
  4. Physical / Logical Bounds: Do the values fall within valid operational limits? 
    if (x <= 0) {
  stop("Argument 'x' must be strictly positive.")
}

docs.title: Combining Validation Checks
docs.text:
Let us build a validated function that computes dissolved oxygen saturation concentration:

calc_do_saturation <- function(temp_c, salinity_psu = 35.0) {
  # Check types
  if (!is.numeric(temp_c) || !is.numeric(salinity_psu)) {
    stop("All arguments must be numeric.")
  }

  # Check scalar lengths
  if (length(temp_c) != 1 || length(salinity_psu) != 1) {
    stop("Inputs must be single scalar values.")
  }

  # Check for NA
  if (is.na(temp_c) || is.na(salinity_psu)) {
    stop("Inputs cannot be NA.")
  }

  # Check domain bounds
  if (temp_c < -2.0 || temp_c > 45.0) {
    stop("Temperature out of realistic environmental range (-2.0 C to 45.0 C).")
  }
  if (salinity_psu < 0.0 || salinity_psu > 50.0) {
    stop("Salinity must be between 0.0 and 50.0 PSU.")
  }

  # Calculation proceeds safely:
  sat_conc <- 14.6 - 0.4 * temp_c + 0.008 * (temp_c^2) - 0.05 * salinity_psu
  return(sat_conc)
}

Alternatively, this also works: 

calc_do_saturation <- function(temp_c, salinity_psu = 35.0) {
  # Check temp_c
  if (!is.numeric(temp_c) ||
      length(temp_c) != 1 ||
      is.na(temp_c) ){
    stop("Argument temp_c must be single numeric value.")
  }

  # Check salinity_psu
  if (!is.numeric(salinity_psu) ||
      length(salinity_psu) != 1 ||
      is.na(salinity_psu) ){
    stop("Argument salinity_psu must be single numeric value.")
  }

  # Check domain bounds
  if (temp_c < -2.0 || temp_c > 45.0) {
    stop("Temperature out of realistic environmental range (-2.0 C to 45.0 C).")
  }
  if (salinity_psu < 0.0 || salinity_psu > 50.0) {
    stop("Salinity must be between 0.0 and 50.0 PSU.")
  }

  # Calculation proceeds safely:
  sat_conc <- 14.6 - 0.4 * temp_c + 0.008 * (temp_c^2) - 0.05 * salinity_psu
  return(sat_conc)
}

Note on || vs | in Conditions: When testing conditions inside an if statement, R provides double operators && (short-circuit AND) and || (short-circuit OR). Unlike & and | (which evaluate across entire vectors element-by-element), && and || evaluate only the first element and stop evaluating further tests as soon as the outcome is decided. Use && and || inside scalar if statements.

docs.title: Q2. Inspect the following function:
docs.text:
calc_dilution_factor <- function(stock_conc, target_conc) {
  if (target_conc >= stock_conc) {
    stop("Target concentration must be strictly less than stock concentration.")
  }
  return(stock_conc / target_conc)
}
What happens if someone evaluates calc_dilution_factor(stock_conc = "100", target_conc = 10)? What additional defensive check is required to prevent this cryptic error message?

docs.title: Flow Control: Conditional Branching
docs.text: Conditional branching allows your code to make decisions, executing different blocks of instructions depending on whether a given condition evaluates to TRUE or FALSE.

docs.title: Syntax of if, else if, and else
docs.text:
classify_water_layer <- function(depth_m) {
  if (depth_m < 0) {
    stop("Depth cannot be negative.")
  }

  if (depth_m <= 200.0) {
    zone <- "Epipelagic"
  } else if (depth_m <= 1000.0) {
    zone <- "Mesopelagic"
  } else if (depth_m <= 4000.0) {
    zone <- "Bathypelagic"
  } else {
    zone <- "Abyssopelagic"
  }

  return(zone)
}

The execution runs sequentially:

  1. R evaluates the condition in the initial if. If TRUE, it executes that code block and skips the rest of the chain.
  2. If FALSE, it moves to the first else if. It tests each subsequent condition until one evaluates to TRUE.
  3. If none of the conditions evaluate to TRUE, the fallback else block executes.

docs.title: Resolving Missing States in Comparisons
docs.text:
A frequent challenge in environmental modeling occurs when an observation might be an established numeric value or missing (NA).

Because comparing an unknown value to a number yields NA (e.g., NA > 5 evaluates to NA), passing NA into a standard if statement will trigger an error: Error in if (x > 5) : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed.

You must explicitly test for missingness using is.na() before performing numeric comparisons:

# Model the establishment of a colonising species arriving at a survey
# site.  The function assumes that species with higher carrying
# capacity K are competitively superior to species with lower carrying
# capacity. Hence, colonisation success depends on a species' carrying
# capacity K compared to the that of the resident species.
resolve_site_occupancy <- function(colonist_K, resident_K) {
  # Scenario A: The habitat patch is completely unoccupied
  if (is.na(resident_K)) {
    final_K <- colonist_K
  # Scenario B: The habitat patch is already occupied
  } else if (colonist_K > resident_K) {
    final_K <- colonist_K  # Colonist outcompetes resident
  } else {
    final_K <- resident_K  # Resident resists invasion
  }

  return(final_K)
}

resolve_site_occupancy(colonist_K = 15.2, resident_K = NA)   # 15.2
resolve_site_occupancy(colonist_K = 12.0, resident_K = 18.5) # 18.5
resolve_site_occupancy(colonist_K = 22.4, resident_K = 18.5) # 22.4

docs.title: Q3. Write a function named clamp_reading that takes three arguments: val, lower, and upper.
docs.text:
1. The function should verify that lower < upper. If not, halt with stop().
  2. If val is strictly below lower, return lower.
  3. If val is strictly above upper, return upper.
  4. Otherwise, return val.

docs.title: Flow Control: Iteration with Loops
docs.text: While R favors vectorized operations for simple mathematical transformations, iterative algorithms, step-by-step simulations, and complex data manipulation require explicit control loops.

docs.title: The for Loop
docs.text:
A for loop executes a block of code once for each element in a sequence:

station_depths <- c(15.0, 45.0, 120.0, 310.0)

for (d in station_depths) {
  cat("Processing station at depth:", d, "meters\n")
}

docs.title: Index-Based Loops and the Vector Pre-Allocation
docs.text: In scientific programming, you routinely use loops to populate a vector or table with calculated outputs.

docs.title: The Anti-Pattern: Dynamic Growth (Do NOT Do This)
docs.text:
# INEFFICIENT AND SLOW:
results <- c()  # Empty vector
for (i in 1:1000) {
  results <- c(results, i * 2)  # Re-allocates memory on every iteration!
}
Every time you call c(results, ...), R has to allocate a completely new chunk of memory in your computer's RAM, copy the entire existing vector into it, append the new value, and delete the old chunk. For large loops, this causes catastrophic slowdowns.

docs.title: The Correct Pattern: Vector Pre-Allocation
docs.text:
Always allocate the complete destination vector with its known final length before entering the loop, and populate values directly by index:

n_steps <- 5
# Pre-allocate numeric vector of length 5 filled with NA:
simulated_profile <- rep(NA, n_steps)

for (i in seq_len(n_steps)) {
  simulated_profile[i] <- 10.0 + 2.5 * (i^1.5)
}

simulated_profile

Safe Indexing with seq_len() and seq_along(): Never write for (i in 1:length(vec)). If vec happens to be empty (length 0), R evaluates 1:0, creating a sequence c(1, 0) that runs two buggy iterations! Instead, always use:

  • seq_len(n): Generates 1:n, or an empty sequence if n == 0.
  • seq_along(vec): Generates indices matching the exact elements of vec, handling empty vectors safely.

docs.title: Controlling Loop Execution: next and break
docs.text:
• next: Immediately skips the remainder of the current loop iteration and advances to the next step.
  • break: Immediately terminates the entire loop, jumping out to the code following the loop block.
measured_temperatures <- c(14.2, -999.0, 16.8, 15.5, -999.0, 18.2)
calibrated_temps <- vector(mode = "numeric", length = length(measured_temperatures))

for (i in seq_along(measured_temperatures)) {
  current_reading <- measured_temperatures[i]

  # Skip corrupted sensor codes (-999.0):
  if (current_reading == -999.0) {
    calibrated_temps[i] <- NA
    next
  }

  # Process valid readings:
  calibrated_temps[i] <- current_reading * 1.02 + 0.1
}

calibrated_temps
# 14.584     NA 17.236 15.910     NA 18.664

docs.title: Q4. Write a for loop that iterates over the integers from 1 to 20.
docs.text: Using next, configure the loop so that it prints only the numbers that are multiples of 3 (hint: use the modulo operator %%, where i %% 3 == 0 identifies multiples of 3).

docs.title: Practical Review Exercises
docs.text: Work through these multi-step exercises in your R script. Focus on translating ecological descriptions into clear, defensive functions and structured, comprehensible code.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Multi-Site Invasiveness & Reserve Threat Scoring Pipeline
docs.text:
Conservation managers evaluate habitat patches for invasive weed colonization risk. The vulnerability of a patch depends on canopy openness, visitor footfall, and distance to the nearest road corridor.

You are provided with records from 6 protected nature reserves:

reserve_names   <- c("Glen_Caladh", "Coed_Cariad", "Cairn_Moss", "Firth_Fen", "Dune_Reach", "Alder_Meadow")
canopy_cover    <- c(0.85, 0.40, 0.15, 0.90, 0.25, 0.60)     # Fractional canopy cover (0 to 1)
visitor_density <- c(12.5, 45.0, 8.0, 3.5, 62.0, 28.0)       # Visitors per hectare per day
road_dist_km    <- c(4.2, 0.8, 12.0, 6.5, 0.3, 1.9)          # Distance to nearest road
is_peatland     <- c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE)  # Peat soils have unique acidity

docs.title: Part A: Patch Vulnerability Index Function
docs.text:
Write a function named calculate_patch_vulnerability that calculates a threat index (V, defined below) for a single site:

calculate_patch_vulnerability <- function(canopy, visitors, road_dist, peatland){
    # your code here
}

The ecological scoring rules are:

  1. Precondition Checks:
    • Verify that 0 <= canopy <= 1. Halt with an error message if not.
    • Verify that visitors >= 0 and road_dist >= 0. Halt with an error message if not.
  2. Base Risk Calculation:
    • Open canopies receive more light, accelerating invasive plant germination: light_score = 1.0 - canopy
    • Roads act as seed dispersal corridors; closer roads increase vulnerability: corridor_risk = 1.0/(1.0 + road_dist)
    • Base vulnerability combines light and road proximity weighted by human traffic: 
      V = (0.6 * light_score + 0.4 * corridor_risk) * (1.0 + 0.05 * visitors)
  3. Soil Modifier:
    • If peatland == TRUE, the acidic soil suppresses most generalist plant invaders. Apply a 40% reduction (V_final = 0.60 * V).
    • Otherwise, V_final = V.
  4. Return V_final.

docs.title: Part B: Reserve Registry and Batch Threat Evaluation
docs.text:
Write a function named audit_reserve_network that processes all candidate reserves:

audit_reserve_network <-
    function(names, canopy, visitors, road_dist, peatland, threat_threshold = 0.75){
        # Your code here
    }
  1. Defensive Check:
    • Ensure that all five input vectors have the exact same length. If not, halt with an appropriate error message.
  2. Iterative Evaluation:
    • Pre-allocate a numeric vector vulnerability_scores of length equal to length(names).
    • Pre-allocate a character vector action_plan of the same length.
    • Using a for loop over seq_along(names):
      • Call calculate_patch_vulnerability() for the i-th site.
      • Store the result in vulnerability_scores[i].
      • Using conditional branching (if / else):
        • If vulnerability_scores[i] >= threat_threshold, assign "Urgent Weed Eradication" to action_plan[i].
        • If vulnerability_scores[i] >= 0.40, assign "Routine Monitoring" to action_plan[i].
        • Otherwise, assign "Low Priority" to action_plan[i].
  3. Assemble Summary Data Frame:
    • Construct and return a data frame with columns:
      • "reserve"
      • "vulnerability"
      • "action"
      • "high_risk" (a logical column where vulnerability >= threat_threshold)

Run the audit on the 6 protected reserves:

reserve_audit <- audit_reserve_network(
  names            = reserve_names,
  canopy           = canopy_cover,
  visitors         = visitor_density,
  road_dist        = road_dist_km,
  peatland         = is_peatland,
  threat_threshold = 0.75
)

reserve_audit

Examine the output data frame. How did the peatland soil modifier affect the vulnerability score of Cairn_Moss relative to Dune_Reach?

docs.title: Exercise 2: The Discrete-Time Logistic Map & Non-Linear Population Regimes
docs.text:
A classic foundation of theoretical population biology is Robert May's (1976) analysis of the discrete-time logistic difference equation: 

x_(t+1) = r x_t (1 - x_t)

Here, x_t represents the population density scaled between 0.0 and 1.0 (as a fraction of carrying capacity), and r is the intrinsic reproductive rate (0 < r <= 4.0).

docs.title: Part A: The Logistic Step Function
docs.text:
Write a function named logistic_step that computes a single step:

logistic_step <- function(x, r){
   # Your code here
}
  1. Minimal Validation:
    • Verify that x >= 0. If violated, halt with stop("x must be non-negative.").
  2. Compute and return the value of x_(t+1), that is, r*x*(1 - x).

docs.title: Part B: Time-Series Generator
docs.text:
Write a function named iterate_logistic_map with the signature:

iterate_logistic_map <- function(x0, r, n_steps){
   # Your code here
}
  1. Validate that n_steps is a single positive integer >= 0. (Tip: A robust way to check for integer values is n_steps == as.integer(n_steps))
  2. Pre-allocate a numeric vector trajectory of length n_steps + 1.
  3. Set trajectory[1] <- x0.
  4. Using a for loop, iteratively call logistic_step() to generate values for t = 1, ..., n_steps.
  5. Return the full trajectory vector.

Test your function: 

traj <- iterate_logistic_map(x0 = 0.2, r = 2.8, n_steps = 50)
length(traj)    # Should be 51
tail(traj, 5)   # Should settle around ~0.6428
plot(traj)      # Gives you a visual impression

docs.title: Part C: Testing for Asymptotic Convergence to a Fixed Point
docs.text:
When small values of r (e.g. r = 2.0), the logistic map converges to a single stable fixed point. For larger values of r, the value of x starts to oscillate.

Write a function named check_fixed_point_convergence that tests whether a trajectory converges:

check_fixed_point_convergence <- function(x0, r, burn_in = 200, tolerance = 1e-4){
    # Your code here
}
  1. Run the map for total_steps = burn_in + 2 steps using iterate_logistic_map().
  2. Extract the last two elements of the evaluation window and compute their absolute difference using the abs() function.
  3. If this differences is less than tolerance:
    • Return TRUE.
    • Otherwise, the system is oscillating or chaotic. Return FALSE.

Test your convergence checker: 

check_fixed_point_convergence(x0 = 0.3, r = 2.6)  
check_fixed_point_convergence(x0 = 0.3, r = 3.2)  
check_fixed_point_convergence(x0 = 0.3, r = 3.8)

docs.title: Exercise 3 (only if you have time): Dynamic Harvest Quotas and Fisheries Escapement
docs.text:
In fisheries conservation, sustainable yield policies often employ biological escapement thresholds. Instead of allowing a fixed annual catch, fisheries managers adjust the permitted quota based on the estimated adult biomass at the start of the season.

Consider a coastal cod stock managed under a three-tier harvest control rule:

  1. Moratorium Tier: If adult biomass B is below the critical threshold B_crit = 1500 tonnes, no fishing is permitted (harvest H = 0).
  2. Proportional Tier: If biomass is between B_crit and the target threshold B_targ = 5000 tonnes, harvest is set to: 
    H = 0.20 x (B - B_crit)
  3. Maximum Sustainable Tier: If biomass is at or above B_targ, the harvest rate is capped at: 
    H = 0.20 x (B_targ - B_crit) + 0.35 x (B - B_targ)

Furthermore, under adverse environmental conditions (e.g., poor marine heatwave years), harvest rates must be reduced by an additional conservation buffer.

docs.title: Part A: Single-Season Harvest Decision Function
docs.text:
Write a function named calc_harvest_quota that accepts the following arguments:

  • biomass: Estimated adult biomass in tonnes.
  • marine_heatwave: Logical scalar indicating whether a severe heatwave occurred during the spawning season (defaults to FALSE).
  • b_crit: Critical threshold (defaults to 1500.0).
  • b_targ: Target threshold (defaults to 5000.0).

The function must execute these steps:

  1. Harvest Determination:
    • Calculate the base harvest H using the three-tier rule above.
    • If marine_heatwave == TRUE and H > 0, apply a 25% reduction to the calculated harvest (H_adj = 0.75 x H).
    • Ensure the final harvest never exceeds the available biomass (H <= B).
  2. Return Value:
    • Return the final permitted catch as a single numeric scalar.

Test your function with the following calls and check the outputs:

calc_harvest_quota(biomass = 1200)                         # Should return 0
calc_harvest_quota(biomass = 3500)                         # 0.20 * (3500 - 1500) = 400
calc_harvest_quota(biomass = 3500, marine_heatwave = TRUE) # 400 * 0.75 = 300
calc_harvest_quota(biomass = 6000)                         # 0.20 * 3500 + 0.35 * 1000 = 1050

docs.title: Part B: Multi-Year Stock Trajectory Simulation
docs.text:
Write a second function named simulate_fishery_trajectory with the signature:

simulate_fishery_trajectory <-
    function(b_start, years, intrinsic_growth = 0.35, carrying_capacity = 8000){
        ...
    }

The function simulates population changes from year t to year t+1 using a logistic growth model with harvest: 

B_(t+1) = B_t + r B_t (1 - B_t/K ) - H_t
where r = intrinsic_growth, K = carrying_capacity, and H_t is determined by calling calc_harvest_quota(biomass = B_t).

Requirements:

  3. Pre-allocate a numeric vector named harvest_history of length years.

    • Determine H_t from the current stock level using calc_harvest_quota(). Store it in harvest_history[t].

    • Extinction check: If calculated biomass falls below 1.0 tonne, set the biomass to 0.0, record the remaining years as 0.0, and terminate the loop immediately using break.

    • biomass: The full trajectory vector.
    • harvest: The vector of catches.
    • collapsed: A logical flag indicating whether the stock collapsed to zero.
  6. Return the list.

docs.text:
Question: What would be the outcome of the code answer <- rep(x = c(42, 24), times = 42)? And what would then be the outcome of the code mean(answer)?

Answer:

The rep() function repeats the vector c(42, 24) a total of 42 times.

answer <- rep(x = c(42, 24), times = 42)
# Result: a vector of length 84 containing: 42, 24, 42, 24, 42, 24, ... (repeated 42 times)

The outcome is a vector with 84 elements (2 elements × 42 repetitions), alternating between 42 and 24.

mean(answer)
# Result: 33

The mean is 33 because: - There are 42 instances of 42 and 42 instances of 24 - Mean = (42 × 42 + 24 × 42) / 84 = (1764 + 1008) / 84 = 2772 / 84 = 33 - Or simply: (42 + 24) / 2 = 33

docs.title: Q6: Open Reading Frame Detection
docs.text:
Question: Write a function which uses regular expressions to detect if a given sequence contains an open reading frame. An open reading frame normally begins with the start codon 'ATG' and ends at one of three possible stop codons, 'TGA', 'TAA' and 'TAG'. The sequence in between these two points is arranged in 3-base codons.

Test it on the following sequences: - ATGGATTTTTAG - ATGGATTTTCTAG - CTAATGGATTTTTGAAT - atgctaaactaa - TCGATTAA

Hint: An open reading frame should always start with the start codon 'ATG' and end with one of the stop codons. Additionally, the length of the entire sequence should be a multiple of 3.

Answer:

# Function to detect open reading frame
is_open_reading_frame <- function(sequence) {
  # Convert to uppercase for consistency
  sequence <- toupper(sequence)

  # Check if sequence starts with ATG and ends with stop codon (TGA, TAA, or TAG)
  # Check if total length is multiple of 3
  # Pattern: ^ATG - starts with ATG
  #          (.{3})* - followed by zero or more triplets of any characters
  #          (TGA|TAA|TAG)$ - ends with one of the stop codons

  pattern <- "^ATG(.{3})*(TGA|TAA|TAG)$"

  # Test the pattern
  result <- grepl(pattern, sequence)

  return(result)
}

# Test on the provided sequences
test_sequences <- c(
  "ATGGATTTTTAG",
  "ATGGATTTTCTAG",
  "CTAATGGATTTTTGAAT",
  "atgctaaactaa",
  "TCGATTAA"
)

# Test each sequence
for (seq in test_sequences) {
  result <- is_open_reading_frame(seq)
  status <- ifelse(result, "Valid ORF", "NOT a valid ORF")
  print(paste(seq, "->", status))
}

Output: 

ATGGATTTTTAG         -> Valid ORF
ATGGATTTTCTAG        -> NOT a valid ORF
CTAATGGATTTTTGAAT    -> NOT a valid ORF
atgctaaactaa         -> Valid ORF
TCGATTAA             -> NOT a valid ORF

docs.title: Q7: Palindromic Sequences
docs.text:
Question: Write a function that assesses whether a given word or phrase is a palindrome. Palindromes are arrangements of words or letters which read the same way whether you read them backwards or forwards, such as the phrase "never odd or even" (if you remove the spaces). In molecular biology, many restriction enzyme sites are palindromic.

Hint: Before starting to code, think about the steps needed to judge if something is a mirror palindrome. Write these steps as comments first, then implement them. Use easy test cases where you know the answer.

Answer:

docs.title: Step 1: Planning (as comments)
docs.text:
# Steps to check if a sequence is a palindrome:
# 1. Convert the input to uppercase (for consistency)
# 2. Remove spaces and special characters (for phrase palindromes)
# 3. Split the string into individual characters
# 4. Reverse the order of characters
# 5. Compare the original with the reversed version
# 6. Return TRUE if they match, FALSE otherwise

docs.title: Step 2: One-off code (testing the logic)
docs.text:
# Test with a simple case
test_word <- "GAATTC"  # EcoRI restriction site - palindromic

# Convert to uppercase
test_word <- toupper(test_word)

# Remove spaces (not needed for this case, but good practice)
test_word <- gsub(" ", "", test_word)

# Split into individual characters
chars <- strsplit(test_word, "")[[1]]
chars
# Result: "G" "A" "A" "T" "T" "C"

# Reverse the characters
reversed_chars <- rev(chars)
reversed_chars
# Result: "C" "T" "T" "A" "A" "G"

# Join back into a string
reversed_word <- paste(reversed_chars, collapse = "")
reversed_word
# Result: "CTTAAG"

# Compare
test_word == reversed_word
# Result: FALSE (GAATTC is not the same as CTTAAG)

# Let's test with a true palindrome
test_word2 <- "GAATTC"
# Actually, for DNA palindrome, we need reverse complement!
# But for simple text palindrome, let's use:
test_word2 <- "racecar"
test_word2 <- toupper(test_word2)
chars2 <- strsplit(test_word2, "")[[1]]
reversed2 <- paste(rev(chars2), collapse = "")
test_word2 == reversed2
# Result: TRUE

docs.title: Step 3: Create the final Function
docs.text:
# Function to check if a word or phrase is a palindrome
is_palindrome <- function(text) {
  # Convert to uppercase for case-insensitive comparison
  text <- toupper(text)

  # Remove spaces and non-alphanumeric characters
  text <- gsub("[^A-Z0-9]", "", text)

  # Split into individual characters
  chars <- strsplit(text, "")[[1]]

  # Reverse the characters
  reversed_chars <- rev(chars)

  # Join back into a string
  reversed_text <- paste(reversed_chars, collapse = "")

  # Compare original with reversed
  is_same <- (text == reversed_text)

  return(is_same)
}

# Test the function
test_cases <- c(
  "racecar",
  "hello",
  "A man a plan a canal Panama",
  "never odd or even",
  "GAATTC",
  "palindrome",
  "madam",
  "step on no pets"
)

# Test each case
for (test in test_cases) {
  result <- is_palindrome(test)
  print(paste(test, "->", ifelse(result, "IS a palindrome", "NOT a palindrome")))
}

Output: 

[1] "racecar -> IS a palindrome"
[1] "hello -> NOT a palindrome"
[1] "A man a plan a canal Panama -> IS a palindrome"
[1] "never odd or even -> IS a palindrome"
[1] "GAATTC -> NOT a palindrome"
[1] "palindrome -> NOT a palindrome"
[1] "madam -> IS a palindrome"
[1] "step on no pets -> IS a palindrome"

Practical 4 - Randomness, Sampling, and Stochastic Simulation
Introduction
docs.text:
In Practicals 1 to 3, all your calculations were deterministic: given the same inputs, your code produced the exact same outputs every single time.

In nature, however, ecological and environmental processes are inherently stochastic. Ecological surveys capture random samples from wider populations; individual organisms face probabilistic risks of mortality, predation, or disease; and environmental drivers fluctuate unpredictably.

Textbooks often treat probability as a collection of abstract formulas. In computational data science, however, the computer is an experimental laboratory where you can observe, manipulate, and experience randomness firsthand. In this practical, you will:

  1. Generate pseudo-random variates using continuous distributions (runif, rnorm) and discrete sampling (sample, sample.int).
  2. Control simulation reproducibility using random number seeds (set.seed).
  3. Model probabilistic events across entire vectors without loops (e.g., survival, detection, extirpation).
  4. Build intuition for rare events and waiting times: how many trials does it actually take for an event with probability 0.05 to occur?
  5. Experiment with the difference between an expectation value and a sample mean: watching independent, noisy histories converge under the Law of Large Numbers.
  6. Apply representations of probability distribution: frequency histograms versus Empirical Cumulative Distribution Functions.
  7. See how the Central Limit Theorem in action: the near-universal distribution of means.

docs.title: 1. Generating Random Variates in R
docs.text: R includes built-in pseudo-random number generators for all standard probability distributions. By convention, random number generating functions begin with the letter r (for random).

docs.title: Continuous Uniform Distribution: runif()
docs.text:
The uniform distribution models situations where any real number within a given interval [min, max] is equally likely to be selected:

runif(n, min = 0, max = 1)
  • n: Number of random numbers to generate.
  • min: Lower limit (defaults to 0).
  • max: Upper limit (defaults to 1).
# Simulate 5 random microclimate humidity proportions between 0.30 and 0.85:
runif(n = 5, min = 0.30, max = 0.85)

If you omit min and max, R defaults to drawing numbers uniformly from the unit interval [0, 1].

docs.title: Continuous Normal Distribution: rnorm()
docs.text:
The normal (Gaussian) distribution produces a bell-shaped curve centered around a specified mean, with spread controlled by its standard deviation:

rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  • n: Number of random observations.
  • mean: Central expectation (defaults to 0).
  • sd: Standard deviation, defining spread (defaults to 1; must be non-negative).
# Simulate adult body lengths (cm) for 6 individual trout (mean = 28.5 cm, sd = 3.2 cm):
rnorm(n = 6, mean = 28.5, sd = 3.2)

docs.title: Discrete Sampling and Random Permutations: sample() and sample.int()
docs.text:
To pick elements randomly from a discrete set or vector, use sample():

sample(x, size, replace = FALSE, prob = NULL)
  • x: A vector of elements from which to choose.
  • size: Number of items to pick.
  • replace: A logical scalar. If FALSE (the default), elements are drawn without replacement (each item can be selected at most once). If TRUE, elements are drawn with replacement (the same item can be picked multiple times).
  • prob: Optional vector of probability weights if elements are not equally likely.
# Simulate drawing 4 tree counts from discrete values between 5 and 20 WITH replacement:
sample(x = 5:20, size = 4, replace = TRUE)

# Randomly select 3 field plots from 10 candidate sites WITHOUT replacement:
site_ids <- paste0("Site_", 1:10)
sample(x = site_ids, size = 3, replace = FALSE)

If you only need to sample integers from 1 to n, the optimized function sample.int(n, size, ...) is faster and concise:

# Pick a single random integer between 1 and 100:
random_station <- sample.int(100, size = 1)
random_station

docs.title: 2. Reproducibility and the Random Seed: set.seed()
docs.text:
Computers cannot produce genuinely random numbers; they use deterministic mathematical algorithms (pseudo-random number generators) that start from an initial number called a seed.

If you do not specify a seed, R initializes its generator from your computer's system clock, giving different numbers on every run. When writing reproducible reports or testing scripts, you can fix the seed using set.seed():

set.seed(42)
runif(3)
# [1] 0.9148060 0.9370754 0.2861395

# Running it again produces different numbers:
runif(3)
# [1] 0.8304476 0.6417455 0.5190959

# Resetting the seed reproduces the exact sequence:
set.seed(42)
runif(3)
# [1] 0.9148060 0.9370754 0.2861395

Rule for Simulations: Use set.seed() at the top of your final script when you need identical, reproducible output for a publication. During exploratory testing, run without a fixed seed to confirm your code behaves properly across different random realizations.
