docs.title: 3. Simulating Random Events with Vectorized Expressions
docs.text: In ecological models, we frequently need to decide whether a discrete event occurs for each member of a population (e.g., does an individual disperse? does a seed germinate? does a patch experience extirpation?).

docs.title: The Uniform Threshold Technique
docs.text:
To simulate an event that occurs with probability p (where 0 <= p <= 1), compare a uniform random number in [0, 1] against p:

Event occurs if: runif(1) < p

Because runif(1) is distributed evenly between 0 and 1, the probability that it falls below p is exactly p.

Crucially, because relational operators (<, <=) are fully vectorized in R, you can simulate thousands of independent events simultaneously without writing a single loop:

# Suppose we have 8 habitat patches, each with an annual extirpation risk of 0.20:
n_patches <- 8
p_extirpation <- 0.20

# Draw 8 random values:
random_draws <- runif(n_patches)

# Vectorized event check:
got_extirpated <- random_draws < p_extirpation
got_extirpated
# [1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE FALSE

docs.title: Heterogeneous Probabilities Across Individuals
docs.text:
This vectorized pattern works equally well when each individual or patch has its own unique risk probability:

# 5 individual fish, each with a different predation risk based on body size:
predation_risk <- c(0.10, 0.45, 0.05, 0.80, 0.30)

# Simulate predation events in a single vectorized step:
eaten <- runif(length(predation_risk)) < predation_risk
eaten

docs.title: 4. Experiencing Randomness
docs.text:
Probabilistic intuition is notoriously deceiving. We tend to expect random processes to look neatly structured or evenly spread out, and we underestimate how much natural clumpiness, streaking, and fluctuation occurs purely by chance.

Let us explore some fundamental phenomena through direct computational experimentation.

docs.title: The Waiting Game: How Long Until Something with p = 0.05 Happens?
docs.text:
In experimental science and statistical hypothesis testing, an event with probability p = 0.05 is often considered "rare" (occurring on average 1 in 20 times).

But what does this mean in practice? Let's find out.

First execute the code below a few times. It outputs TRUE in 5% of cases.

runif(1) < 0.05

Now, let's automate this. Let's write a while loop that counts how many independent trials it takes until a 'rare' event (p = 0.05) occurs for the first time:

trial_count <- 0
event_occurred <- FALSE

while (!event_occurred) {
  trial_count <- trial_count + 1
  # Test if event occurs on this trial:
  if (runif(1) < 0.05) {
    event_occurred <- TRUE
  }
}

cat("Event occurred on trial number:", trial_count, "\n")

Run that code block in your console 5 to 10 times in succession. Notice the dramatic unpredictability.

docs.title: Repeated Simulation: The Waiting-Time Distribution
docs.text:
To see the full pattern, let us automate this experiment across 1,000 independent simulated runs:

simulate_waiting_time <- function(p = 0.05) {
  trial_count <- 0
  while (TRUE) {
    trial_count <- trial_count + 1
    if (runif(1) < p) {
      return(trial_count)
    }
  }
}

# Run 1000 independent replications:
n_reps <- 1000
waiting_times <- rep(NA, n_reps)

for (i in seq_len(n_reps)) {
  waiting_times[i] <- simulate_waiting_time(p = 0.05)
}

# Plot waiting times across all 1000 successive runs:
plot(waiting_times, pch = 16, col = "grey",
     xlab = "Simulation Run", ylab = "Trials Until First Event",
     main = "Waiting Times Across 1000 Independent Realizations")
abline(h = 20, col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)  # Theoretical average wait (1 / 0.05)
legend("topright", legend = "Expected Mean (20 trials)", col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

Look at the plot:

  • Each point represents one complete simulation run. Notice the dense cloud of points hugging the bottom axis: in a large proportion of runs, the event occurred within the first 5 to 15 trials.
  • More than half of the runs finish below the theoretical average wait of 20 trials (the red dashed line).
  • At the same time, look at the erratic spikes shooting high above the average: occasionally, you wait 60, 80, or even more than 100 trials!

Now, let us group these 1,000 individual runs into a frequency histogram to view the aggregated distribution:

# Visualise the distribution of waiting times:
hist(waiting_times, breaks = 30, col = "blue", 
     xlab = "Number of trials until first event",
     main = "Waiting Times for p = 0.05 Event")
abline(v = mean(waiting_times), col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", legend = paste("Mean =", round(mean(waiting_times), 1)), 
       col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 2)

Takeaway: Randomness exhibits so-called geometric waiting times. Even when the expected average wait is 20 trials, waiting times are heavily skewed. Something that happens at random with 5% probability easily happens quite soon or after quite a long time.

docs.title: 5. Expectation vs. Mean:  The Invisible Attraction of Expectation
docs.text: After having built intuition about the concept of "probability", let's develop intuition about another concept that is central to statistics: the "expectation value". Conceptually, the expectation value of a random variable (such as the outcome of a measurement) is the average over a very large number of equivalent measurements. But what does this really mean?

docs.title: Building a "Mystery Loaded Die"
docs.text:
Copy the code below and into your RStudio script and evaluate it to define the function create_mystery_die. 

create_mystery_die <- function(n_faces = 6) {
  ## This function outputs a mystery die with n_faces faces.
  if(!is.numeric(n_faces) || is.na(n_faces[1]) || n_faces[1] < 2)
    stop("Bad value for n_faces.")
  n_faces <- as.integer(n_faces[1])
  randomness  <- runif(1)
  set.seed(as.numeric(Sys.time()) * randomness)
  weights <- runif(n_faces, min = 0.5, max = 1.5)
  secret_probs <- weights / sum(weights)
  secret_expectation <- sum((1:n_faces) * secret_probs)
  set.seed(randomness * .Machine$integer.max)
  function(n = 1) {
    sample(1:n_faces, size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = secret_probs)
  }
}

The function uses some advanced R trickery and I won't explain how it works. But what it does is the following:

Calling create_mystery_die() returns another function. This function simulates a loaded die, that is, a die that will give you one of the outcomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 each time you 'roll' it, but it won't give them with the exact same probability. Nobody, not even I, knows what the probability of each outcome is!

This is the situation that almost every scientist doing empirical research faces. You will face it as well when doing your MSc project: when you collect data or do measurements, your are getting random outcomes each time according to rules that nobody knows. And yet you need to conclude something useful from this randomness to submit your thesis!

Now, instantiate your personal die:

my_die <- create_mystery_die()

Try out your die: 

my_die(1)   # Roll once
my_die(1)   # Roll again
my_die(1)   # Roll another time
my_die(10)  # Roll 10 times
Can you see from the outputs that the die is loaded?

docs.title: The Sample Mean
docs.text:
For a die that is not loaded, we can compute the "average" outcome of rolling it. Because all faces of the die have the same probability, the "average" outcome can be calculate by averaging over the outcomes: (1 + ... + 6) / 6 = 3.5. But, as you know, the outcome of each roll is random, so simply averaging over six rolls won't give 3.5. We can use the sample.int() function to demonstrate this. Try it out several times: 

six_fair_rolls <- sample.int(n = 6, size = 6, replace = TRUE)
six_fair_rolls
mean(six_fair_rolls)

The outcome is hard to distinguish from that using a loaded die. Compare with the result of running the following code several times: 

six_loaded_rolls <- my_die(6)
six_loaded_rolls
mean(six_loaded_rolls)

To get, for a fair die, an average close to the value 3.5 that we expect, we need to average over many, many rolls. Try the following a few times: 

mean(sample.int(n = 6, size = 10^6, replace = TRUE))

Here's the crucial observation: by averaging over many unpredictable outcomes, we obtained a pretty well reproducible outcome. This reproducible outcome from averaging over many, many samples is called the expectation value.

We can use this method to show that our mystery die is loaded. Try the following a few time: 

mean(my_die(10^6))

You can see that the expectation value of rolling my_die is also reproducible and clearly different from that of a fair die. The difference is that for the fair die we could compute the expectation value using some maths. For my_die we could not. We had to obtain it from averaging over many measurements. So, if you'd be studying my_die for your MSc thesis, you could:

  • Report the expectation value you find.
  • Observe that the expectation value is clearly different from that for a fair die.
  • Conclude that my_die is not fair, but rather tends to give lower [or higher] values.
  • However, you'd have to roll the die 10^6 = 1,000,000 times!

docs.title: Watching Means in Multiple Parallel Universes Converge
docs.text:
Here's the problem: you usually can't make 10^6 = 1,000,000 measurements for your MSc thesis!

So, how many measurements do we rally need to get hold of an expectation value?

Let us simulate rolling the mystery die 2,000 times. But instead of watching just one sequence, let us simulate 5 independent parallel universes running side by side, and plot the sample means we get as data accumulates:

n_rolls <- 2000
n_universes <- 5

# Set up an empty coordinate space:
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, n_rolls), ylim = c(1.5, 5.5),
     xlab = "Number of Die Rolls (Sample Size n)",
     ylab = "Cumulative Running Mean",
     main = "5 Independent Realizations of My_Die")

# Assign distinct colours to each parallel history:
palette <- c("lightblue", "darkgreen", "darkorange", "purple", "brown")

# Pre-allocate a vector to record the final asymptotic estimates:
final_estimates <- numeric(n_universes)

# Simulate and overlay each running trajectory:
for (k in seq_len(n_universes)) {
  rolls <- my_die(n = n_rolls)
  # Here we use a trick to compute all n_roll means in one line:
  running_mean <- cumsum(rolls) / seq_len(n_rolls)
  lines(running_mean, col = palette[k], lwd = 1.4)
  final_estimates[k] <- running_mean[n_rolls]
}

Write down what you observe: 

## Your notes here

How many samples do you recommend to take to get reliable estimates of expectation values? 

## How many samples:

Reflect on what you have just witnessed:

  • The sample mean is an empirical measurement. It is a random number. It is noisy and changes with every sample.
  • The expectation value is not an average of data. It was fixed the moment my_die was created by create_mystery_die, before a single die was ever rolled.
  • The expectation value is like an invisible attractor towards which sample means move for large sample sizes. The Law of Large Numbers is the physical guarantee that, as individual random observations accumulate, their collective historical average is captured by this invisible attractor.

docs.title: Zooming In: Small-Sample Size Experiments
docs.text:
To understand why field biology and conservation surveys are so difficult, let's do some experiments with only 100 rolls of our die:

# Re-plot focusing strictly on small sample sizes (n = 1 to 100):
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 100), ylim = c(1.5, 5.5),
     xlab = "Number of Die Rolls (Sample Size n)",
     ylab = "Cumulative Running Mean",
     main = "The Small-Sample Trap: First 100 Rolls")

for (k in seq_len(n_universes)) {
  rolls <- my_die(n = 100)
  running_mean <- cumsum(rolls) / seq_len(100)
  lines(running_mean, col = palette[k], lwd = 1.4)
}

Notice how wide the spread remains even at n = 50. When researchers report "the average body mass is 3.2 kg" from a field survey of 30 animals, this may sounds as if the sample mean accurately reflects the underlying expectation value. As your plot demonstrates, that intuition can be overconfident.

docs.title: Q3. The Expectation Value of a Continuous Uniform Distribution
docs.text:
If a variable is drawn uniformly from continuous values between 10.0 and 20.0 (runif(n, min = 10.0, max = 20.0)), every real value in that interval is equally likely.

  1. What is the expectation value of this continuous distribution?
  2. Write a script that simulates 4 independent histories of 1,500 uniform draws between 10.0 and 20.0, and plots their running means (as above) simultaneously on a single graph.
  3. Overlay a horizontal line indicating the expectation value using abline(h = [your value here]). At approximately what sample size n do all 4 independent histories consistently stay within +/- 0.2 of the expectation?

docs.title: 6. Histograms and Empirical Cumulative Distribution Functions
docs.text:
The expectation value is not the only property of random variables (such as measured values) that is accessible only by taking many, many, samples - more than we can typically take in ecology.

The full information about at random variable is given by the distribution of its values. There are two ways to think about a distribution. Mathematicians are interested in what they call the distribution function: 

F(x) = (probability that observation <= x)
Practitioners usually ask: what is the probability for my observation to be in the range between x1 and x2. We can obtain this from F(x) as 
(probability that observation > x1 but <= x2) = F(x1) - F(x1).
From a limited number of samples, we can estimate the distribution using either a histogram or the empirical cumulative distribution (given by the proportion of observations <= x).

Since these representations convey the same information, we call them collectively the distribution of the observable or random variable.

docs.title: Q4. Experimenting with empirical distributions
docs.text:
The code below generates both the empirical distribution and the histogram of some mock random data. Experiment with increasing (e.g., by a factor 10 or 100) the values of n_samples and of the breaks parameter of hist to reveal the true distribution and compare it with the empirical small-samples estimates obtainable from 100 samples. 

## Set up two-plot layout:
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))

## Generate some interesting mock data
n_samples <- 100
sim_data <- rnorm(n_samples, mean = c(5, 5, 15), sd = c(3, 2, 3))

## Get data min and max for plot alignment
data_range <- range(sim_data)

## 1. Empirical Cumulative Distribution Function:
n <- length(sim_data)
plot(x = sort(sim_data),         # Ordered data plotted on x axis!
     y = seq_len(n_samples)/n_samples,
     type = "S",                 # Plot data as a step-function
     main = "Empirical Cumulative Distribution",
     xlab = "Measured Value (x)", ylab = "Proportion <= x",
     xlim=data_range) 
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)  # Lowest possible proportion
abline(h = 1, lty = 2)  # Highest possible proportion

## 2. Frequency Histogram:
hist(sim_data, col = "lightgrey", breaks = 10,
     main = "Histogram (Binned Density)", xlab = "Measured Value",
     xlim=data_range)

## Reset plotting layout to single panel:
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

Using sim_data from above:

  1. Use mean(sim_data <= 12.0) to calculate the exact proportion of data points that are <= 12.0.
  2. Verify where this point falls on the vertical axis of your empirical distribution function.

docs.title: 7. The Central Limit Theorem
docs.text:
Now, let's look at distributions not of single observations, but of means of observations.

Below, we will compute means of many samples of the uniform distribution. We also compute means of random variables given by x^p, where x is uniformly distributed and p is some fixed number. As you will see, x^p is not uniformly distributed.

To compute one such mean, we use mean(runif(sample_size))^p. In order to obtain the distribution of these means, we compute 10,000 of them using replicate(10000, mean(runif(sample_size)^p).

docs.title: Q5. Experimenting with The Central Limit Theorem
docs.text:
Using the code below, experiment with changing the value of p (to change the distribution of the 'measurements' we are averaging over) and changing the sample_size of value x^p that enter out mean. (N.B.: a sample_size of 1 gives you the distribution of x^p itself.) 

## Set up two-plot layout:
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))

p <- 1 # try, e.g., 1, 3, 1/2, etc,
sample_size <- 1 # try, 1, 2, 3, ... 10, 100, 1000

## Generate and plot histogram
random_means <- replicate(10000, mean(runif(sample_size)^p))
histo <- hist(random_means, breaks = 50, plot = FALSE)
plot(histo, xlab = "Mean over samples", main = "Zoom")  
plot(histo, xlab = "Mean over samples", main = "Full Range", xlim = c(0,1))  

## Reset plotting layout to single panel:
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
The shape of the distribution you find for large samples sizes is called the normal distribution or Gaussian distribution or bell curve. The function rnorm introduced above generates random numbers with precisely this distribution.

docs.title: Q5b. Convergence to the Normal Distribution
docs.text:
Going back to the last script, find out at about what sample size the distribution of the mean visually becomes a normal distribution. Compare this with this with sample sizes we required above to find accurate estimates of the expectation value of my_die.

So, this is our saviour! While we need many thousands of samples to reconstruct the distribution or expectation value of a measurement (making this practically impossible), we know that the mean over a reasonably small number of samples is approximately normally distributed. This observation is the starting point of the mathematics underlying most statistical methods used in ecology.

The 'normal distribution' is actually a family of distributions with two parameters: the central value, called the mean of the normal distribution, and it's width, quantified by the standard deviation.

We already know how to estimate the mean of a distribution. The function sd estimates the standard deviation: 

sample_small <- rnorm(10, mean = 0.3, sd = 1.5)
sample_large <- rnorm(10000, mean = 0.3, sd = 1.5)

sd(sample_small)  # Some noisy estiates
sd(sample_large)  # Close to 1.5

## Note the following:
sd(sample_large)^2
sample_mean <- mean(sample_large)
mean( (sample_large - sample_mean)^2 )
var(sample_large)  # Variance 'var()' is the square of the standard deviation

## And so:
sqrt( mean( (sample_large - sample_mean)^2 ) )
sd(sample_large)
Because of the approximate relation above, the standard deviation is also called the root mean square (RMS) deviation from the mean. Make sure you can identify the 'root', the 'mean' and the 'square' in the last code block above.

docs.title: Exercise 1: The Mark-Release-Recapture Lincoln-Petersen Simulator
docs.text:
In wildlife biology, ecologists estimate the size of an elusive animal population (N_true) using the Lincoln-Petersen mark-recapture method:

  1. In the first sampling session, M animals are captured, marked, and released back into the wild.
  2. After allowing time for marked animals to mix into the population, a second sample of C animals is captured.
  3. The number of marked individuals recaptured in the second sample is recorded as R.
  4. The estimated total population size (N_hat) is calculated as: 
    N_hat = (M * C) / R

Because recapture is a stochastic process, R fluctuates randomly across surveys, causing N_hat to vary.

docs.title: Part A: Simulating a Single Recapture Survey
docs.text:
Write a function named simulate_recapture_survey with the signature:

simulate_recapture_survey <- function(n_true, m_marked, c_captured) {
  # Your code here
}

The function must execute these steps:

  1. Defensive Validation:
    • Verify that n_true, m_marked, and c_captured are single numeric integers >= 1.
    • Verify that m_marked <= n_true and c_captured <= n_true. If violated, halt with stop().
  2. Population Representation:
    • Represent the population of size n_true as an integer vector: marked individuals are represented by 1, and unmarked individuals by 0.
    • Construct this vector using rep(): 
      population <- c(rep(1, m_marked), rep(0, n_true - m_marked))
  3. Simulating Capture:
    • Draw a sample of size c_captured from population without replacement using sample().
    • Count how many marked individuals were recaptured by summing the sample (R).
  4. Estimation:
    • If R > 0, compute N_hat = (M * C) / R.
    • If R == 0 (no marked animals were recaptured), the formula divides by zero; return NA.
  5. Return N_hat as a single numeric scalar.

Test your function with a known population:

simulate_recapture_survey(n_true = 500, m_marked = 80, c_captured = 60)

Run this line three or four times. Notice that even though the true population is fixed at 500, the estimate fluctuates.

docs.title: Part B: Evaluating Estimator Bias and Variance
docs.text:
Now, write an iterated simulation script to evaluate how well the Lincoln-Petersen estimator performs:

  1. Fix the parameters: n_true = 1000, m_marked = 150, c_captured = 100.
  2. Using a for loop or the replicate function, generate a vector pop_estimates with 500 population estimates using simulate_recapture_survey.
  3. Calculate the proportion of surveys that failed due to zero recaptures (mean(is.na(pop_estimates))).
  4. Compute the average population estimate across all valid surveys (mean(pop_estimates, na.rm = TRUE)). How close is this to the true value of 1,000?
  5. Plot a histogram of the valid estimates and overlay a vertical red line (e.g., using abline) marking the true population size (1000).

docs.title: Exercise 2 (if you can't get enough): Forest Gap Disturbance & Tree Recruitment Dynamics
docs.text:
In temperate rainforests, canopy trees persist for centuries until catastrophic windthrow storms create light gaps, triggering new sapling recruitment.

We will simulate a stand of 100 canopy trees over annual time steps.

docs.title: Problem Formulation
docs.text:
• Stand State: The stand is represented by a numeric vector tree_ages of length 100, where each element is the age of the tree occupying that canopy position.
  • Annual Disturbance Risk: In any given year, an extreme windstorm occurs with probability p_storm = 0.08.
  • Tree Mortality:
    • If a windstorm occurs in year t, older trees are vulnerable to windthrow: any tree with age > 60 years suffers an 80% mortality rate (each older tree dies independently with probability 0.80).
    • Younger trees (age <= 60) have flexible trunks and survive the storm.
    • In years without a storm, trees simply age by 1 year.
  • Gap Regeneration: When a tree dies, its position is immediately colonized by a new seedling of age = 1 year.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Write a function named simulate_forest_year that updates the stand across a single annual time step: 

    simulate_forest_year <- function(tree_ages, p_storm = 0.08) {
  # Your code here
}

    • Validate that tree_ages is a numeric vector with length >= 1 and contains no negative values.
    • Check if a storm occurs this year by testing runif(1) < p_storm.
    • If a storm occurs:
      • Identify indices of vulnerable trees where tree_ages > 60.
      • For each vulnerable tree, determine if it dies using vectorized random uniform numbers: runif(n_vulnerable) < 0.80.
      • Reset the age of trees that died to 1.
      • For all trees that survived, increase their age by 1.
    • If no storm occurs:
      • Increment the age of all trees by 1.
    • Return the updated tree_ages vector.

  2. Write a multi-year simulation function named run_forest_simulation: 

    run_forest_simulation <- function(initial_ages, n_years, p_storm = 0.08) {
  # Your code here
}

    • Pre-allocate a numeric vector named mean_age_trajectory of length n_years + 1.
    • Record the initial mean stand age in mean_age_trajectory[1].
    • Using a for loop over 1:n_years, iteratively update the forest stand and record the mean tree age at each step.
    • Return a named list containing:
      • final_stand: The vector of tree ages at the end of the simulation.
      • mean_ages: The annual trajectory of mean stand age.

  3. Run a 150-year simulation starting from an even-aged mature stand: 

    initial_stand <- rep(50, 100) # 100 trees, all 50 years old

sim_results <- run_forest_simulation(initial_ages = initial_stand, n_years = 150, p_storm = 0.08)

# Plot mean stand age trajectory over time:
plot(sim_results$mean_ages, type = "l", col = "forestgreen", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Time (years)", ylab = "Mean Canopy Age (years)",
     main = "Forest Stand Age")

Examine the trajectory plot. What causes the pronounced structure in the variation of mean age over time?
